utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is the day when the Prosecution is going to start making their closing arguments. And let me wish you a good afternoon to you all, including those who are not here; that is, Mr. Pusic, for instance. And let me use this opportunity to welcome here a new Petkovic Defence counsel, Mr. Zoran Ivanisevic. Furthermore, in terms of scheduling: On Wednesday, we were scheduled to sit in the morning, but we are going to sit in the afternoon because the Tolimir case requested a change, for reasons known to the Tolimir Chamber. I hope this will cause no inconvenience to anybody. Since it's going to happen on Wednesday, I wanted to let you know today already. Furthermore, all those who will have an opportunity to speak in the next hours or weeks to come should speak slowly, please, for the interpreters to be able to render their thoughts faithfully. And if ever we were to run into problems, that time would be taken out of the allotted time to each of the parties. Also, the TribuNet site failed to mention the fact that we were going to have our final closing arguments, whilst it was stated for Charles Taylor and his case. It must be an omission, because I know they're overworked. Still, they mention that there were a lot of Croatian journalists coming to attend the final arguments. Through me, the Trial Chamber wishes to recall that closing arguments by all parties should not be a repetition of submissions made in closing briefs. The Trial Chamber urges the parties to focus on the key issues in this case. When the Defence teams start making their final arguments, each Defence team will first tell the Trial Chamber whether the accused planned to make statements for a maximum of 30 minutes each out of the 5 hours allotted to each Defence team. The Trial Chamber recalls that should an accused request the right to speak, he will speak last, at any rate. Furthermore, if the accused do not wish to speak, the time that we gave to each of the accused may not be given back to their counsel. The Trial Chamber recalls that the time allotted to a Defence team may not be given to another Defence team. And the Trial Chamber reserves itself the right to rule on reasoned rebuttal or rejoinder motions, if any, to the closing arguments once the Trial Chamber has heard all of the closing arguments. So all this being said, you know that this is a direct result of the orders we issued and decisions we handed down. And I'm going to give the floor to Judge Trechsel because he wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: First, one observation. In the meantime, probably while our President was speaking, the internet, in fact, announces the final pleadings in the Prlic case. The second point is: There has been a little mistake in the transcript. It's found on, I think, line 19 of page 2. There are two questions of cessation of time. One is: One Defence cannot give time that they do not use to another Defence. But when a Defence decides that the accused will not, within the frame of their presentation, take the floor, they dispose of the full time, in fact. They don't lose any time in that case. That was, I think, a slip of the tongue or maybe even a misprint. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now everything has been said. I think Mr. Scott is ready to go. I can see him at the rostrum. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do apologise. Perhaps before my learned friend starts, we could get the assistance of the Court staff, because our LiveNote for this Defence team is not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sure, the staff is going to come in a minute. But let's not prevent Mr. Scott from starting, because the transcript, as such, is working.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Counsel, the accused, Your Honours, good afternoon. May it please the Court. On October 23rd of 1993, Mufida Likic was a 14-year-old Muslim girl living in Stupni Do. She got up at about 7.00 that morning, had breakfast with her mother, her aunt, her two-year-old cousin. After doing the breakfast dishes, she went outside to pile some firewood. Her mother took their only cow to a nearby field to graze. It must have seemed like a normal day. It must have seemed like most other days. But a short time later, all of that came suddenly to an end, and Mufida's life changed forever. There was a sound of gun-fire and then a grenade exploding. The shooting increased dramatically, seeming to come from all directions. She ran to the basement of her house with her father, sister, and aunt. By this time, bullets were breaking the small basement windows. Mufida said, in her own words, the windows, quote, "were blown to smithereens. Bullets were entering the basement, where they were lying on the floor." Over the course of the next hour, all in the midst of gun-fire, other Muslim women and children came to the basement to hide, many of them still wearing their night clothes. By the end of an hour, there were 11 Muslim women and children hiding in the basement. Fearing the arrival of the attacking soldiers at some of the nearby houses, the group of 11 decided to run to the basement of another nearby house, to Kemal's house. When they arrived in the basement there, there was Kemal's wife and small child. Now there were 13 Muslim women and children. At one point, Mufida was able to look out of the basement and saw her house and barn on fire. Now the attacking soldiers approached Kemal's house, and the group decided to flee again. Once outside, Mufida saw her part of the village completely on fire. Stupni Do was in flames. As she continued on to Kada's house, she was wounded by a gun-shot to her left side. When she arrived in Kada's basement, she found her sister, Medina, her aunt, Hatidza, and her neighbour, Nezveta Likic, already there. There was a small pit in the basement that was only a few feet deep, which was used to store potatoes. The four Muslim women huddled in that pit, with Mufida behind and at the bottom. After a time, they heard men's voices outside, and then there were two explosions in the basement. A man came into the basement, saw them, and yelled to someone outside, I have found three balijas women, apparently not seeing Mufida, who was behind and under the others. There was then the sound of two men in the basement, and they were cursing and swearing. There was a sudden burst of gun-fire, and Mufida felt the body of her sister slump heavily on top of her. After a time, it was quiet again inside the basement. This is what Mufida said: "I called Nezveta, Hatidza, and Medina in a low whisper. There was no response. I called my sister's name again and touched her hand. She did not respond. I crept out of the pit. Nezveta, Hatidza, and Medina still sat crouching in the pit, their heads bent over, their chins touching their chest. I tried to shake the body of my sister, but she was dead. All three of them were dead." Mufida's story goes on for some time after that; how she continued to move about the village and the surrounding woods, seeing again her entire village on fire. She and other Muslim women and children eventually made their way through the woods to the road to Dabravine, where they were found by an UNPROFOR unit two days later on the 25th of October, 1993. Searching through all the civilians and all the people who had fled the area, Mufida found her mother and told her that Nezveta and Hatidza and Medina were dead. Her mother fainted, woke up, and then cried for a long time. Witness BQ -- and I'll hasten to add that while this witness has a pseudonym, he testified primarily in open session, with face distortion. Witness BQ was a Muslim man who told the Court how he was held by the HVO at Dretelj for approximately 58 days in the summer of 1993. The exhibits that are on the screen in front of you, P09718, P09719, and P09721, are photographs which will remind the Chamber of the Dretelj camp and what it looked like, the buildings or the hangars where Witness BQ and other Muslim men were held by the HVO. He told us that about 500 to 600 Muslim men were kept in that tunnel. Most of them were from Prozor, but there were also men from Central Bosnia and other parts of Herzegovina. The Chamber heard how, when the detained men received any food, "it was so awful that maybe it was better that we had none. I would never have given it to my dogs, my pigs, or my cattle." As for amounts, it was so small, one little loaf of 700 grams was divided into pieces for 17 people, and this soup that we got was just boiled over a fire. It was so hot, just off the fire, and we had 10 to 20 seconds to eat it. I don't think anybody could have held that dish with food for more than 20 seconds." When Witness BQ and other Muslim men were released from Dretelj on or about the 28th of August, 1993, the HVO took them in buses from Capljina to Vrda, and from Vrda they had to walk to Dreznica. Many of the men were exhausted and in poor health. Many of them could hardly walk at all. Some collapsed on the way, suffering additional injuries. The witness, himself, said that he could barely stand and only barely made it from Vrda to Dreznica. And the Chamber and those around the courtroom are now seeing some of the photographs of the Muslim men who were released from Dretelj on that day. Witness BQ never saw at doctor at Dretelj, was not aware of any medical care ever being provided there. The bandages that can be seen on some of the released men were only given to them, only placed on them, after they arrived at Dreznica by the Red Cross or UNPROFOR. Witness BQ weighed approximately 94 kilograms before he was detained, and when he was released from Dreznica, he weighed 37 kilograms. It could not have been a diet that he had ever wished for. The Chamber will recall the testimony of Dr. Jovan Rajkov, who was a surgeon in the East Mostar War Hospital in 1993, who told the Chamber about the work of that make-shift hospital, especially starting on the 9th of May, 1993, about the horrible conditions in that hospital and the limited medical supplies. The Chamber will recall a number of video-clips involving the hospital, which the Chamber may wish to review. Dr. Rajkov drew a stark contrast to the hospital in West Mostar: "It wasn't under a siege, it wasn't under a blockade. If they needed something, they could bring it in, install it, whatever." Dr. Rajkov testified about the treatment of a large number of civilian women and children for wounds and injuries, including bullet wounds and from shelling, and identified two of the known sniper locations in Stotina and in the glass building. He testified that ambulances were specifically targeted by shelling and sniping and how a substantial number of the hospital's own medical staff were either killed or wounded in 1993. How do we get to these sad and horrible events? What brought us here. What happened in those parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina that some people called Herceg-Bosna? What happened that brought us to this case, that brought us to this trial? The Prosecution submits that at the core of what happened, what led to and caused these events and others, was the joint criminal enterprise charged in this case, an enterprise to establish a Greater Croatia as set out in the indictment, quote, "to politically and militarily subjugate, permanently remove, and ethnically cleanse Bosnian Muslims and other non-Croats who lived in areas on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were claimed to be part of the Croatian Community and later Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and to join these areas as part of a Greater Croatia, whether in the short term or over time, and whether it is part of the Republic of Croatia or in close association with it, and, as part of this, quote, "to engineer the political and ethnic map of those areas so that they would be Croat-dominated, both politically and demographically." The Prosecution respectfully submits, Your Honours, that there are four fundamental points. The starting points are actual permanent points, the Prosecution suggests, if the Chamber will continually look to, it would provide help in analysing the evidence in this case. First of all, what was this all about? In a nutshell, the Greater Croatia, Herceg-Bosna Banovina, was about establishing a Croat space, with borders, controlled by Croats, demographically and politically, that looked, felt and sounded like Croatia. That's about as succinct a statement as the Prosecution believes it can make about what this was all about. Now, let's talk about each of those elements, the important elements, when I said there were four points, in more detail. First, this was a top-down project or agenda or programme. Greater Croatia was a top-down project driven by a relatively small, politically -- excuse me, political and military elite, a political class of Croat nationalists who had a particular ethnic and political vision. This is the story of a nationalist faction that took control of the HDZ and set out to implement Franjo Tudjman's vision of a Greater Croatia. These six men were not just a group of individuals who were caught up in something coming from the bottom up, from the grassroots, as some say. No, this was top down. This project was imagined, planned, prepared, decided, driven, administered, implemented and carried out from the top down. And these men, these men over here, were among its designers, architects, builders, and executioners. Judge Trechsel hit the head -- hit the nail on the head in an intervention on the 2nd of June, 2009, transcript page 41035-36, in responding to some points being made by Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: "Mr. Praljak, I'll put to you something which you will consider as provocative, probably. And it's not at all my intention to provoke, but I think in sheer honesty, I have to tell you, listening to you this afternoon, I start wondering whether this war, that is presented as a war of the Croatian Narod or people, for their popular rights, these people's rights, in fact, is not something that the people wanted, but that a small stratum, a class, a caste of politicians and military and other very nationalistic minded people wanted, and which they then whipped through, not being pushed from underneath, from the popular, from the grassroots; but, on the contrary, pulling out the grass to throw it into the war, to some extent." The Prosecution submits that's exactly what happened here. This was top down. Everything that happened, the ultimatums, the expulsions, the destruction, the putting Muslim women and children on buses, the transit visas, taking them to a third country, destroying the mosque, destroying communities, was all top down. For confirmation that the Greater Croatia/Herceg-Bosna project and the crime committed were a top-down enterprise, we need look, in fact, no further than the words of the accused. Prlic confirmed -- Mr. Prlic confirmed the Herceg-Bosna plan, adopted, proclaimed and supported by Zagreb: "They were also using the opportunity to address the public and say to the public that everything was being done and all the preparations were being done to defend Herzegovina, which was only partly correct, partly true. HVO, between themselves, they created another plan, which was adopted and proclaimed and supported by Zagreb, which was also the political centre of power. So the goal and the main point of that plan was to defend the territory and also -- excuse me, and possibly also attach it to the Republic of Croatia." Mr. Prlic likewise confirmed that during the course of the war and following, he had been implementing Tudjman's instructions. In a meeting with Tudjman in Zagreb on the 20th of June, 1998, Prlic said : "I do not belong to any line. I have been implementing what you were telling me all the time." To which Tudjman replied: "Well, it is for sure that you are the most intelligent one within that structure." Praljak confirmed that he was implementing the same top-down policy with Tudjman, Prlic mand Stojic: "I was implementing the policies of the Croatian state. "My policies were parallel to the policies of the Republic of Croatia and the policies of Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, Bruno Stojic, Jadranko Prlic, and all of the others." Mr. Praljak's own words. Mr. Prlic confirmed that the Croat-Muslim war was directed by Herceg-Bosna's political leaders. "... the war was fought by political leaders through the Main Staff of the HVO, actually through the military organs." Petkovic confirmed that the Herceg-Bosna civilian leaders control the HVO military, stating: "... objectives are set by politics rather than the military. The military must implement these decisions." Praljak again confirmed political control of the HVO military: "A political decision has an absolute priority over a military decision. You cannot conduct the creation of a state --" let me repeat that, " ... the creation of a state from 20 centres, but from one." Who were these central political figures that were exercising control over the military? Well, Petkovic told us that as well. Petkovic confirmed that the three highest political or civilian authorities concerning Herceg-Bosna's military and defence matters were Boban, as president of the Herceg-Bosna, Prlic, as president of the government, and Stojic, as head of the Defence Department, with the Defence Department being part of Prlic's government. Petkovic confirmed, in fact, that Stojic was, quote, "my minister." Prlic confirmed that the HVO committed -- excuse me, the HVO military committed crimes: "It is quite clear that HVO military units, members of military units, committed crimes, and, therefore, HVO military authorities were responsible and should be held responsible, should be answerable for that." Herceg-Bosna was top down; Tudjman, Susak, others in Zagreb, these men and others. Another important component or element of the whole project was territory. The Croat-Muslim war, arising from the Greater Croatia project, was all about territory, about Croatia and some Croats regaining all or much of a territory that had once been known as the Croatian or Hrvatska Banovina in 1939. We will talk more about that, but that is the fundamental territorial element. To use other terminology that has come up in the course of the trial, the Croats wanted their own sovereign space, a sovereign area of geography, real estate with borders. It wasn't the plan or it wasn't enough to just establish some abstract, philosophical idea of Croat-ness. No, you wanted to have a piece of territory, a piece of ground to call your own. To make it real, to put it on the map, you needed a space with borders. But that also wasn't enough. You also had to have demographics. Putting borders or lines on a map would not necessarily accomplish your goal of your own sovereign space unless you, indeed, had or could gain control within those borders or on that territory. Assuming that the system of government on that territory was going to be something broadly like a democracy, something broadly like each adult having an equal vote, you needed to have a majority of those voters. Or to put it differently, your group needed to be in the majority. If those pursuing a Herceg-Bosna or banovina put borders around it, put lines on a map, but inside those borders, the Muslims in all or large parts of it were still in the majority, were still in control politically, demographically, culturally, you hadn't accomplished very much. They could still out-vote you, they could still do what they wanted to do, so to speak, and that was not the purpose of Herceg-Bosna. What's the point of having territory if you don't actually control it? At the same time, a demographic advantage, by itself, was not helpful. You might have an overall demographic advantage spread out over a large territory, but still no physical space that is, quote, "your own." The Herceg-Bosnans needed or wanted both territory and demographics. Having put those two elements, territory and demography, on the table, I think Mr. Praljak confirmed for us the importance and the application of these two elements. I'm going to get to some Praljak testimony in a moment, but I'm going to introduce that by referring first to some testimony of the British journalist Ed Vulliamy. Vulliamy interviewed Boban in Grude in mid-April of 1992, and this is what, according to Vulliamy's testimony in this courtroom, Boban told him: Boban made it clear that he did not and could not recognise the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, nor could he recognise Sarajevo as its capital. The reason he gave was that the Constitution guaranteed the rights of individuals, but not of people, and the word he used for people was "narod." Forgive me if I'm mispronouncing that - which is an important word because it means people as an ethnicity. He then went on to describe in some detail how he wanted the various "narod" Serbian, Muslims, and Croatians to be divided within Bosnia by a system of what he called cantons or provinces, and how one group of these cantons or provinces would be specifically Croatian. He talked about how Herceg-Bosna was connected to Croatia, and the words he used were "culturally, spiritually, and economically," and he said that -- excuse me -- and he said that Herceg-Bosna had been separated from Croatia by what he called, quote, "unfortunate historical circumstances." This testimony about what Boban said was then put to Mr. Praljak by my colleague, Mr. Stringer: "Q. Now, two questions on this for you, General. "First of all, Boban's views expressed to Mr. Vulliamy in this conversation in August of 1992 --" I apologise. I misspoke earlier and said "April." I should have said "August of 1992." "... that Boban's views are essentially a mirror image of the views of President Tudjman, aren't they, these cultural and spiritual links between Herceg-Bosna, Croatia, and the unfortunate historical circumstances that resulted in separation from Croatia? "So wouldn't you agree with me, based on what we've seen already, that Boban's views were essentially the same views as President Tudjman on this issue? "A. Well, I'm in an awkward situation here. I don't know -- I don't know how I can answer to such a question. These are the positions of Mate Boban he put forward at a meeting with Mr. Vulliamy. I don't know what they spoke about. I only know what Vulliamy says that they spoke about. But based on that account, I can say that everything is all right. Boban speaks about cantons. This idea was present all the time in our minds." Praljak spoke further about this, Mr. Stringer pursuing further: "Q. I'm putting to you, sir, that what that means is that you're rejecting the unitary state system of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you are advocating instead a separateness based on autonomy and territory for different peoples; isn't that true? "A. Yes, that's correct, that's what I advocated then. I advocate that today. So I stand by what I said. I fully support my words. "Q. Now, General, I want to come back again to your testimony about your objective here for an autonomous area, where Croats would be an absolute or relative majority. Would you agree with me that such an area, were it to exist, would have to have an identifiable border? "A. That is correct. "Q. Would you agree with me that such an area that you envisaged, that you're speaking about here, would not be a temporary entity under Bosnia-Herzegovina or within Bosnia-Herzegovina, but what you wanted was a permanent autonomous area for Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina? "A. Yes, it was supposed to be permanent." The fourth element and final element was, if I can coin the phrase, "Croat-ness." What you finally wanted -- what the Herceg-Bosnians finally wanted, not just territory, not just demographics, but Croat-ness. This territory, this space with borders and demographics, needed to be Croat. It needed to sound, look, and feel Croat; Croatian culture, Croatian symbols, Croatian flags, Croatian anthems, Croatian currency, Croatian curriculum, Croatian language, Croatian driver's license, Croatian citizenship. It had to look and sound and feel like Croatia. The four critical elements the Prosecution submits to you: Top-down, territory, demographics, Croat-ness. With those four elements in mind, I want to address the case at some length, and especially in response to various parts of especially the Prlic, Stojic, and Praljak final briefs as to a variety of issues that largely started and occurred during the period 1990 to the end of 1992, which will bring us to the largest part of the indictment in 1993. Franjo Tudjman's views about Croatia's borders, as they existed in 1990, and his obsession with restoring the Croatian banovina of 1939, were well known, as he, himself, stated these views on many occasions. In his 1981 book "Nationalism in Contemporary Europe," Tudjman said that the creation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a separate Republic in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had made Croatia's territorial and geographic position, quote, "unnatural, in the economic sense, and unsuitable, in the administrative sense." According to Tudjman, it was entirely artificial to separate Bosnia and Herzegovina from Croatia, since Bosnia and Herzegovina were historically linked with Croatia, in his view, and they together comprised an indivisible geographic and economic entity. That is quoting his book that I cited a moment ago. The solution, according to Tudjman and others, was to add to Croatia's existing borders a territory that had been known as the Croatian or Hrvatska banovina. This large area was the result of a 1939 agreement between the Serbian-Yugoslav prime minister, Cvjetkovic, and the Croat leader, Vlado Macek, which created a large Croatian territory encompassing much of Bosnia and Herzegovina and almost all the former Triune Kingdom of Croatia, Slovenia, and Dalmatia. While the agreement only lasted until Germany and Italy invaded Yugoslavia in April 1941, Tudjman and others idealised Croatia's expanded banovina borders and longed to restore the banovina by annexing large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia. Josip Manolic, who was the prime minister of Croatia in 1990-1991, a member of Croatia's Defence and National Security Council in 1993, and president of Croatian Parliament's Upper Chamber in 1994, came and testified. And I know it's been some time ago now, but hopefully some of these witnesses will come back to all of us as we continue to review and study the evidence. Mr. Manolic confirmed in his ICTY testimony that Tudjman was, quote, "obsessed with this idea of the banovina creation, and he described the realisation of the banovina borders as the main goal of Tudjman's policy. The principle idea of the Croatian state policy, according to Manolic, was the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina independently from any other circumstances. The, quote, "annexation of Herzegovina to Croatia" was really the guiding idea of the Croatian state policy. Tudjman's own foreign minister, Mate Granic, wrote in his book, "Foreign Affairs Behind the Scenes," quote: "Tudjman's obsession was to re-create the Croatian banovina which had been established in 1939, according to which Herzegovina and parts of Central Bosnia and the Bosnian Posavina were joined to Croatia. The president often told me that the banovina was the best solution." Tudjman's views concerning Muslims, not surprisingly, were consistent with his views towards Bosnia. In a meeting with Herceg-Bosna representatives in December 1993, Tudjman said that the Croats had fought the Muslims for three centuries and that it was the Muslims who had brought Croatia to the brink of disaster. Tudjman explained that the ordinary Bosnian Croat preferred the Orthodox Christian Serbs to the Muslims, quote, "because he is a Christian, after all." US Ambassador Peter Galbraith had a number of meetings with President Tudjman and testified that Tudjman often referred to the 1939 banovina. President Tudjman believed that Bosnia-Herzegovina would not and should not continue, that Bosnia should not and would not continue as a sovereign, independent state, and that a substantial part of Bosnian territory should become territory of the Republic of Croatia. Not only that, but Galbraith told us that Tudjman often spoke favorably of population exchanges, population transfers, that this had been something that had been done through history and there was nothing so unusual about moving populations, exchanging population, and that was clearly part of Tudjman's vision. He explained to Galbraith which territories should become part of Croatia, and even produced a map showing Bosnia being divided right down the middle, was Galbraith's words, right down the middle. Mostar, in Tudjman's view, was a Croatian city. It was the capital of the Croatian territory in BiH, and as far as Tudjman was concerned, the Muslims could not claim Mostar as theirs. Now, those who were or who would become the political and military leaders of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO in 1991 and 1992, and would lead the persecution and ethnic cleansing against the Muslims in 1992 and 1993, shared Tudjman's views about the banovina and establishing Croatian political, military, and demographic control in a Croatian space. The roles of the accused in this case are set out in the Prosecution's final brief and will be discussed further in the course of the Prosecution's closing submissions as to individual accused. We will pause, however, to talk about where Mr. Boban fit in this picture. Like Tudjman, Mate Boban believed that Herceg-Bosna had been separated from Croatia by unfortunate historical circumstances and saw the banovina as a model for Herceg-Bosna and a precedent for its joinder with Croatia. Boban ran for office as an HDZ-BiH candidate in the November 1999 elections in Bosnia and received fewer votes than the moderate Croat, Stjepan Kljuic. On 18th of September 1991, he became vice-president of the HDZ BiH Crisis Staff. Together with Dario Kordic, Boban shared the important meeting of the Travnik and Herzegovina HDZ Regional Communities on 12 November 1991, which called for a, quote, "decisive and active policy which should lead to the realisation of our eternal dream, a joint Croatian state." The meeting's conclusions, signed by Boban and others, called for the proclamation of a Croatian banovina, quote, "as the first step on the road to the final solution of the Croatian question and the creation of a Sovereign Croatia in its ethnic and historical, now-possible borders." It was no accident that when Boban and Franjo Boras met with Bosnian-Serb leader Radovan Karadzic in May 1992 in Graz, that the Herceg-Bosna position was stated in terms of the 1939 banovina. Your Honours, I'm reluctant to proceed if we're having technical interference. I'm not blaming anyone, but it makes it difficult to have the Chamber's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you can continue. The transcript is working. We only have some problems with LiveNote. What's important is listening to you and reading the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. According to the ECMM official Ray Lane, Boban and his political associates wanted to live in a Greater Croatia, and their major political direction was unification with the Republic of Croatia. Boban was a strident Croat nationalist and had little regard for other ethnic groups, but was more closely aligned with the Serbs and their concepts for Bosnia than the Muslims. The Croatian foreign minister Mate Granic we referred to earlier described Boban as a, quote, "very narrow minded man, full of hatred for the Bosniaks." Witness Suad Cupina testified that Boban told him in June 1992 that he had no intention of recognising the BiH leadership in Sarajevo or the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that Herceg-Bosna was intended to be a state for Croats. By January 1993, Boban was implementing a policy of moving Muslims out of areas that he considered Croat under the Vance-Owen proposals and moving Croats from other parts of Bosnia into the so-called Croat areas. In an 8 March 1993 meeting with Tudjman, Susak, and others, Boban said that Bosnia and Herzegovina would soon cease to exist, and confirmed that Herceg-Bosna and HVO -- and the HVO were tools to create a greater Croatia: "It all came down to us --" Excuse me: "It is all down to us. No one is going to put freedom in our lapse. There is no such Croatia that will bring freedom to us, because we are an essential part of Croatia. You know that we, in our policies, we all know these policies precisely, and let me not repeat them again here. "Every Croat from Bosnia and Herzegovina has the right to Croatia as much as President Franjo Tudjman, but we have to keep and create Croatia there, and it is our -- that is our task that you know very well." The British diplomat David Owen complained to Tudjman in June 1993 that Boban treated Mostar and Travnik as if they were his. Boban derided the value of cease-fire agreements and also blamed the Muslims for violation. Boban said that the three groups, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, could not live together for the foreseeable future, and he said: "Better to say the truth. We are at war over territory and borders." The Croatian leader Manolic testified that in implementing Tudjman's banovina policy, Boban did nothing without the knowledge of President Tudjman. In a 24 August 1993 Croatian TV programme, Boban characterised his relationship with Franjo Tudjman in the following way: "Franjo Tudjman is the president of Croats throughout the world, and thus also the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The political programme of the HDZ, of which he is president, is the programme that I and my associates have been implementing systematically in the territory of BiH. I therefore listen to Franjo Tudjman to the extent I listen to the programme of the HDZ, of which he is president, which is also the extent to which I respect him and accept all of his rationalities as the president of all Croats in the world." On 2 September 1993, Tudjman ordered Boban to deal with the HVO prison camps, which were harming Croatia's image. Beyond that, by late November 1993, the continuing international pressure on Croatia arising from Herceg-Bosna's behaviour caused Tudjman to effectively remove Boban as president, although he stayed in that position until approximately the 11th of February, 1994. This development had no effect on Boban's views, and he remained Tudjman's loyal soldier. Boban told a British journalist, in the latter part of 1993: "We will become a part of the Republic of Croatia. That is the aim of the Croats in BiH." When Boban and Jadranko Prlic met with Karadzic and Ratko Mladic on the 3rd of February, 1994, Boban told the Serb leaders: "We shall never agree to less than a BiH union of three republics. The boundary determinations between Serbs and Croats is the condition for peace in the Balkans. The most important task is to destroy the legitimacy of BH." All of this -- Your Honour, all of this evidence is fully consistent and supports the following adjudicated facts: One, Franjo Tudjman's nationalism and his desire to annex a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina was apparent to Lord David Owen, to whom President Tudjman staked his claim that 17.5 per cent of Bosnian territory should revert to a republic with a Croatian majority. President Tudjman aspired to partitioning this neighbouring country, Bosnia-Herzegovina. The aspirations of Franjo Tudjman to annex Croatian regions of Bosnia persisted throughout the conflict. "There is no doubt that the Republic of Croatia and the HZ-HB were pursuing the same ultimate goals; namely, the incorporation of Croatian provinces of Bosnia and Herzegovina into a single Croatian state. The foundation of the Croatian Democratic Union -- or community, excuse me, or union, the HDZ, was laid in February in 1989 in Zagreb with Franjo Tudjman making the opening speech. In Croatia's April 1990 multi-party elections, the HDZ garnered more votes than any other party, and Tudjman was elected president. Throughout the 1990s, the HDZ dominated Croatian politics, and Tudjman remained president until his death in late 1999. With the establishment of the HDZ in Croatia, it next turned its focus on creating the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In this regard and concerning Zagreb's overall relations with what became Herceg-Bosna, a group known as the Herzegovina Lobby, led by the Croatian Defence Minister Susak, who had been born and raised in Siroki Brijeg, played a prominent role. The HDZ leadership in Zagreb identified a physician from Sarajevo, Dr. Davor Perinovic, and invited him to lay the foundation of the HDZ BiH. Unfortunately, it turned out a short time later that Mr. Perinovic was discovered to have Serbian ethnicity, making him unqualified, apparently, to head the HDZ BiH, and he was removed by the party leadership. In the same month of September 1990, the Bosnian Croat Stjepan Kljuic was travelling through Zagreb, where, at Tudjman's request, they discussed Kljuic taking over as party leader. The HDZ Main Board met in Zagreb and decided to make Kljuic the new BiH party head, and he became that in September 1990. The Chamber has heard about the elections in Bosnia in 1990; the three principle parties being, as the two you've heard -- or one you've heard already, the HDZ BiH, the other party would be the Party of Democratic, the SDA, considered by many to be primarily a Muslim party, and the Serbian Democratic party or SDS. On 18 November 1990, the first multi-party elections for the republic and legislature were held. Out of a total of 240 seats, the SDA won 86 seats, the SDS won 72, the HDZ BiH won 44. Among the HDZ BiH candidates, Kljuic won the most votes, more than Boban. The three parties filled the seven positions on the BiH Presidency as follows: Stjepan Kljuic was a Croat member; Franjo Boras, Croat member; Alija Izetbegovic, Muslim; Fikret Abdic, Muslim; Biljana Plavsic, Serb ; Nikola Koljevic, Serb; and Ejup Ganic, who consisted with, or allowed by Bosnian law, identified himself as a, quote, "Yugoslav" and filled that position. The parties formed a coalition government with Alija Izetbegovic named president of the Presidency; the Croat, Jure Pelivan, made prime minister; and the Serb, Momcilo Krajisnik, made president of the Parliament. That takes us, at least to some extent, up to the time of March 1991 and the meeting in Karadjordjevo. It is an adjudicated fact that Franjo Tudjman's aspirations to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina were, quote, "displayed during the confidential talks between Franjo Tudjman and Slobodan Milosevic in Karadjordjevo on 30 March 1991 on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Other related adjudicated facts established by the Trial Chamber are, quote: "The views that President Tudjman harboured territorial ambitions in respect of Bosnia and Herzegovina, despite his official position to the contrary, is strengthened by reports of discussions held between Tudjman and Milosevic, against the backdrop of the break-up of the Yugoslav federation in 1991. "Follow Karadjordjevo, Franjo Tudjman opined that it would be very difficult for Bosnia to survive and that the Croats were going to take over the Banovina plus Cazin, Kladusa, and Bihac. "Franjo Tudjman also said there would no longer be a Muslim region within the former Yugoslavia, that it would constitute only a 'small element of the Croat state.'" Now, questions have been raised by some of the Defence about whether -- well, we know there was a meeting at Karadjordjevo, but what was actually said. But, Your Honours, Ambassador Okun, the senior Croat leader, again, Manolic, and Kljuic all confirmed and discussed Karadjordjevo and its implications and consequences for the facts of this case. I will not go into the content of the testimony, because it was in closed session, but I especially commend to you the detailed testimony of Witness AR. In the book "Origins of the Catastrophe," the American diplomat Warren Zimmerman, who was the last US ambassador to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslav, described what Tudjman told him about the meetings with Milosevic: "Tudjman admitted that he had discussed these fantasies about an Islamic fundamentalist Bosnia with Milosevic, and they agree that the only solution is to divide up Bosnia between Serbia and Croatia. Magnanimously, Tudjman said he didn't insist on a 50-50 division. 'Let Milosevic take the larger part; he controls it anyway. We can do with less than 50 per cent. We're willing to leave the Muslims a small area around Sarajevo. They may not like it, but a stable Balkans is possible only if there's a change in Bosnia's borders, no matter what the Muslims think. There's nothing sacred about those borders. Bosnia isn't an old state, like Croatia, which once extended all the way to Zemun (a western suburb of Belgrade.'" Zimmerman talking: "Listening to Tudjman, I realised I had to abandon diplomatic niceties. In our view, Izetbegovic was neither a radical fundamentalist nor a threat to anybody. The United States would strongly oppose the break-up of Bosnia. 'Nobody who wants to do this can count on any assistance from us. There will be war in Bosnia if you try to divide it.'" Take note of that, in terms of the concept of foreseeability, the concept of planning, the concept of knowing what was around the corner. "There will be war in Bosnia if you try to divide it. Don't you think the Muslims will react? What you propose ignores the rights of a large share of Bosnia's population." The problem of Bosnia -- that was Tudjman's own term, "the problem of Bosnia." At an important meeting of Croatia's Supreme State Council on the 8th of June 1991, Tudjman confirmed, again, his discussions with Milosevic and his continuing view that Croatia's, quote, "impossible borders were largely due to Bosnia's historically absurd borders," and he explained to those assembled, quote, "how to solve the problem of Bosnia." "... as you know, in the beginning the Serbs said that if there was to be a confederal alliance, they would not accept the current borders ... because of the Serbs living outside Serbia in Bosnia and Croatia ... "So this is the reality that we cannot overlook. Also, gentlemen, if we opt for Croatia's independence, either within an alliance or total independence, Croatia's borders, such as they are today, are absurd, they are impossible, in the sense of administration and trade, let alone as regards any kind of protection of these borders of Croatia. "Therefore, from our point of view, no less than from the Serbian, there is the problem of -- there is a need to find an essential solution to the problem, isn't that so, because the establishment of Bosnia, the borders of BH after World War II, are historically absurd, a resurrection of a colonial creation from the period between the 15th and 18th century." Tudjman informed those present, and again we're talking about Croatia's Supreme State Council, that there would be, quote, "talks on the problems, problem of Bosnia, that is the problem of boundary determination and the borders of the Republic of Croatia." Tudjman made it clear that solving, quote, "the problem of Bosnia," and gaining, quote, "realistic borders for a sovereign Croatia Bosnia," were the core problems. "The solution to the problem of Bosnia," Tudjman said, "lies in what was said there in the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if we achieve that, then we could possibly look for a basis for an alliance of sovereign republics and states. I think we shall achieve this, because this is equally in the interest of Serbia and Croatia, while the Muslim component has no other exit than to accept this solution, although it will not be easy to find the solution, but essentially that is it." Now, there are a series of meetings throughout mid-1991 which we're not going to take -- and you'll probably be happy to know we're not going to go through all of those. But the evidence clearly demonstrates there is an ongoing series of meetings in Bosnia and Herzegovina involving the Boban-Kordic-Boras faction, and these communities that are set out, the two largest ones that are most relevant to this case, being the Regional Community of Travnik and the Regional Community of Herzegovina, headed by Kordic and Boban respectively, these communities are moving all through 1991 closer and closer to unification together and closer and closer to the establishment of Herceg-Bosna. Throughout this time, there is a growing split between Boban, Boras, Kordic, on the one hand, and people like Kljuic and the more moderate Croats, on the other, and there is a continuing dialogue - well, "dialogue" is a nice way of putting it - a debate, friction, argument going on throughout mid-1991 as to the proper course for the HDZ BiH, with these factions battling for control. What is interesting for the Chamber to note in this respect is: At the same time, and we're stepping off the HDZ for a moment, but while this is all going on, the Serbs are doing essentially exactly the -- doing or have done exactly the same thing. While all of these events were taking place, the Serb and Bosnian Serb leadership of the Serb political party, the SDS, in the spring of 1991 were also establishing various illegal regional groups or communities or municipalities. The first of these, the community of municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina, was formed in April 1991, and the community of the municipalities of Eastern and Old Herzegovina, and the community of the Romanija municipalities, was formed in May. The BiH Assembly took immediate action in opposition to these structures, issuing a recommendation in April 1991 that all efforts to organise regional entities or associations of municipalities cease. The various actions, however, continue. These projects continued over time. They then evolved into something called the Serbian autonomous districts or SAOs, and it's important to note that the Defence's own expert witness, Mr. Jurcevic, said this was, in his words, "evident on these facts" that, quote, "that the national concept of the structure of the Serbian people in BH was an integral part of the Greater Serbia project and that it was in an advanced phase of operational/political implementation as early as 1991." Again, Mr. Jurcevic described the SAOs and the Serb organisations as, quote, "a prerequisite for an integral part of the armed aggression and occupation of BiH." It's interesting that when we had a Croat expert looking at what the Serbs were doing, that Croat expert who came and testified on behalf of the Defence, which he had every right to do, of course, it was very clear to him that these were illegal entities, all the tools of -- all being used to accomplish a greater Serbia. But all of a sudden when what the Croats were doing and what happened with Herceg-Bosna, when you put those same facts in front of him, well, that's different, it's not greater Croatia, no, I wouldn't go that far. So it works for the Serbs; didn't work for the Croatians, according to Dr. Jurcevic. By this time on November 1 1991, the BiH Constitutional Court ruled that the Serb entities were illegal and annulled them; in particular, to the extent that the association had attempted to exercise powers related to defence and military matters, including, quote, "social self-protection." The Court stated that it was the republic which regulated such matters. The Court also found the actions procedurally defective, in that most of these decisions to establish these Serb entities were taken pursuant to an alleged, quote, "emergency procedure," quote, "often without announced agenda without the presence of the council members of Croatian and Muslim nationality." What a surprise. Now, I note the date of the Court decision, 1 November 1991. The BiH Constitutional Court says the Serb entities are illegal and they are annulled. Only 18 days later, on the 18th of November, 1991, Herceg-Bosnans declare the existence of Herceg-Bosna, after the BiH Constitutional Court decision, after the government of BiH has already said these are illegal organisations. Now, with the Serb developments in mind, let's continue back to these efforts of the Herceg-Bosnans, Boras, Boban, Kordic, and the others to establish Herceg-Bosna. We've already made reference to the important meeting on the 12th of November, 1991, in Grude of the Herzegovina and Travnik Regional Communities, and they reached the following conclusions that day: "The Herzegovina Regional Community and the Travnik Regional Community stand by their conclusions ... that the Croatian people of these regions continue to uphold the unanimously accepted decisions and conclusions adopted during consultations with President Dr. Franjo Tudjman on 13 and 20 June 1991 in Zagreb. Proceeding from the conclusions of the above-mentioned meetings," and again that's the meetings on the 13th and the 20th of June, "on the basis of those two meetings, these two regional communities have jointly and unanimously decided that the Croatian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina must finally carry out a decisive and active policy which should lead to the realisation of our centuries-old dream, a joint Croatian state. "In order for this historical goal to soon become our reality, these two regional communities request the commencement of activities to formulate and issue legal and political documents (the proclamation of a Croatian banovina in BH, a referendum on accession to the Republic of Croatia, et cetera) as the first stage -- as the first stage on the road to the final settlement of the issue and the creation of a sovereign Croatia in its ethnic and historical (now possible) borders." Six days later, on Monday, 18 November 1991, in Grude, Kordic, Bozo Rajic, and others proclaim the existence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, stating in Article 1 that it. "... shall be established as a political, economic, and territorial integrity." Article 3 made Mostar a Muslim-majority city in a Muslim plurality municipality, the seat of the Croatian community. And Article 2 said that the HZ-HB shall be composed of the following 30 municipalities, only 12 of which actually had a Croat-majority population. The Chamber will see in front of it a list of the 30 municipalities and their demographic composition, in terms of majority or plurality, based on the 1991 census. Out of the 30 claimed municipalities, Your Honours, only 12, less than half, actually had a Croat majority, actual majority; not plurality, but more than 50 per cent. As an overlay of the maps plainly show, and not surprisingly, the borders of the declared Herceg-Bosna and those of the Croatian Community of Bosanska Posavina in north-east Bosnia matched almost perfectly the borders of the 1939 banovina, with the addition of areas such as Vares, Kakanj, and Jajce, none of which had a Croat-majority population. We saw these maps on the very first day, if we can all remember back far enough to the opening statement in April of 2006. The first map, map number 3, shows the Croatian Communities of Herceg-Bosna and Bosanska Posavina. The next map, map number 5, shows the overlay of banovina of 1939 on the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The next map shows the overlay of the banovina with the Croatian community, the red line being the borders of the banovina. And we see that Herceg-Bosna even -- actually claimed a couple of areas -- several areas that were outside the historical banovina. And then in map number 9, the ethnic composition based on the 1991 census, and we see the ethnic composition of the municipalities claimed by Herceg-Bosna. Now, the Prosecution submits, Your Honours, that it doesn't take the proverbial rocket science when you look at the ethnic composition of these areas and see that there was an inherent conflict at work. Go back to the four principles, or at least two of them, territory and demographics. Well, if the area in blue -- the area in the blue border is your territory, you've got a serious problem with demographic control, because you've just claimed to be yours territories where you are not in the majority. As a large body of evidence confirms, including the evidence of Kljuic, the constitutional expert from Slovenia Ribicic, Donia, and Tomljanovich, the establishment of Herceg-Bosna was the creation of a Bosnian-Croat para-state in BiH, the introduction of a para-state administration. It was a mono-national community with mono-national bodies that merged from a mono-party formation, the HDZ BiH, or, more accurately, a particular faction of that party. At no time had there been a referendum or any free and democratic election for either the Croats or the Muslims, or any other non-Croats, in Bosnia and Herzegovina in which a majority of any ethnic group had voiced its support or approval for the establishment of Herceg-Bosna. This was a sheer fiat by a small faction of the HDZ BiH, like Boban, Boras, Kordic, and others, and with these men joining that group. There was never a popular -- not even the Croats, themselves, ever voted for this, let alone the Muslims. There were no open and democratic elections held to the organs. No one ever elected -- no popular vote ever elected anyone to Mr. Prlic's HVO government. Bosnia and Herzegovina was still legally part of Yugoslavia, and its republican bodies, including the Presidency, the government and parliament, all were clearly functioning. And that's an important statement. I want to pause there for a moment, because what you've heard over the last number of years is, Well, we had to create Herceg-Bosna because BiH wasn't functioning, the authorities weren't functioning. In November of 1991, there was still no war, primarily. There had been skirmishes, unfortunate skirmishes, but there was no large-scale war in Bosnia. There was no large-scale armed conflict there. Businesses were operating, taxes were collected, schools were in session, the trains were running, and mail was being delivered. The authorities were not not functioning at the time that Herceg-Bosna declared its existence. Shortly after Herceg-Bosna was announced, both the BiH government and Constitutional Court condemned it. An opinion issued by the BiH Ministry of Justice and Administration on the 20th of November, 1991, just two days later, so that all the actions that Herceg-Bosna had purported to take were, quote, "illegal and illegitimate, contrary to the Constitution and the interests of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and all its citizens." A 23 November 1991 report concerning the work of the Constitutional Court said that the creation of separate communities and other entities had continued since the Court's previous report on the 6th of November and that the Court, by late November, was responding to, quote, "only the most violent violations of constitutionality and legality." And quote: "Forming of the creation community of --" excuse me, "municipalities, Herceg-Bosna, and a similar community based in Brcko, represent an anti-constitutional act and an illegal attempt to change the constitutional order." It is an adjudicated fact in this case that the HZ-HB was founded with the intention that it should secede from Bosnia-Herzegovina with a view to unification with Croatia. Mr. President, I'm about to change to another topic. And looking at the clock, it might be a convenient time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well, absolutely. Let's have a break. We'll have our traditional 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. A few weeks after the declaration of Herceg-Bosna's existence on the 18th of November, 1991, there was an extremely important meeting in Zagreb on the 27th of December, 1991. If I had to tell anyone, Judges, or anyone else interested in this case, if you had to read maybe 12 documents or a dozen documents or so in full, and you could only read about that many, this would be one of them. It is at this meeting on the 27th of December, 1991, chaired by Tudjman, that the two factions of the HDZ BiH come to Zagreb and essentially plead their case. You have the Boban-Kordic-Boras faction and you have the Kljuic-Doko-Markesic, faction, if you will, if you want to call it that, sitting before the master and arguing in which direction all of this should go. Tudjman's there with his senior advisers and the leaders of the Bosnian branch of his party. Kljuic -- as I said, Kljuic is there, Jerko Doko, who was then at that time -- I believe at that time was already the minister of defence in Bosnia, a Croat, Ivan Markesic, and then you had Boban, Kordic, Boras and others. Kljuic continued to fight and press for a single, multi-ethnic, independent, and sovereign BiH, while Boban's group was fighting for the creation of the banovina and their own sovereign Herceg-Bosna space. Four days earlier, the party's hard-liners had met in Tomislavgrad and had excluded Kljuic from that meeting. They made their position clear in item 2 in the minutes of this earlier meeting in Tomislavgrad, which was the same position they expressed now to Tudjman, even purporting to speak -- and this is a recurring theme, something that I'd ask the Judges to be mindful of. This is a recurring theme, with Boban and the others claiming to speak on behalf of all Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, with absolutely no mandate or basis for doing so, claiming that they had, quote, "confirmed the will of the entire Croatian people of Herceg-Bosna expressed on 18 November 1991..." Well, as I said to you before the break, there was no election, there was no vote. This was one faction of the party. Mr. Kljuic, in the 1990 elections, the moderate, had received more votes than Boban. This was the take-over of the party by one faction, without any election, and simply your basic power struggle. In contrast to that position, which I should say further, and I pause, forgive me, the Boban group continued to say and read out the minutes of the Tomislavgrad meeting and said that it was this declaration -- excuse me, the declaration of Herceg-Bosna would serve as, quote, "a legal basis for the entry of these territories into the Republic of Croatia." In contrast, Kljuic continued to push for a single, unified, and sovereign BiH. Kljuic argued, among other things, that the problem of banovina and the problem of Herceg-Bosna was that a large portion of the Croatian population in Bosnia was left outside that area, with Kljuic noting that only 14 of Herceg-Bosna's claimed 30 municipalities had a Croat-majority population. I think Kljuic was slightly off in his counting, but close. By the meeting's end, it was clear where Tudjman stood and where the party was headed, with Boban's faction clearly in control. Tudjman openly chastised Kljuic for supporting Bosnia's sovereign existence: "Bosnia-Herzegovina should not be taken as something God-given which must be preserved, and we must especially not forget how harmful it is, because of the creation of Bosnia and Herzegovina Croatia has been put in an impossible situation regarding its territory." Indeed, Tudjman said Bosnia's continued existence was against Croatia's interest: "The survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent and sovereign estate, even if possible, is in any case against the interest of the Croatian state and makes impossible the normal territorial establishment of the Croatian state, and creates conditions for the disappearance of what remains of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina today." Mark those words. The continued existence, the survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is contrary to the Croat national interest. Tudjman continued on: "All of history has shown that Bosnia and Herzegovina is no solution for the Croatian people. "We said that for tactical reasons we were in favour of a sovereign Bosnia as long as it existed, but there is no longer a sovereign Bosnia. The Serbs have split off." Again, not really a true statement at that time. "It seems to me, therefore, that just as we have taken advantage of this historic moment to establish an independent, internationally-recognised Croatia, I believe that it is time that we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders ..." Tudjman made it clear that Bosnia's break-up -- complete break-up was the real goal, saying that: "Not even some sort of cantonisation, with the continuing existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would mean for us the solution, which is the solution of demarcation; that is, borders." There can be no doubt that from the meeting, Tudjman meant the borders between Croatia and Serbia that would be drawn in BiH, with Croatia's desired, quote, "demarcation" being the banovina borders. "I think we have had sufficient experience, what with World War II and this war, that without demarcation between Croatia and Serbia, there can be no political solution, no removal of the threat of war in the future. The state of Croatia cannot survive such as it is, but a Croatian state, even with the borders of the banovina, could, not to mention if these borders were improved on." Now, here we can see Tudjman even going a step further. Now he's saying, you know, Not only might we get the banovina, but we might even be able to improve on that. And, indeed, Tudjman was convinced that Croatia, in the course of Bosnia being divided up, might obtain not only the banovina, largely in the form of Herceg-Bosna's claimed municipalities, but also the overwhelmingly Muslim-populated municipalities in Bosnia's north-west corner, including Bihac. In the end, an agreed carve-up with the Serbs would leave Bosnia's Muslims with a small, quote, "statelet" around Sarajevo. In apparent reference to his previous conversations with Milosevic, Tudjman told the meeting: "Why not accept this offer of demarcation when it is in the interest of the Croatian people, the Croatian people here in this republic and the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because I do not see a single reason -- a single serious reason against it." But Tudjman, Boban and the others knew full well that changing the lines on a map was only part of the solution. Achieving a real Greater Croatia required a dominant Croatian demography which, in turn, would require population movements. At least behind the closed presidential doors, Boban made no bones about it. The founding municipalities of HZ-HB now have a population which, according to the census, is 55 per cent Croatian, 27 per cent Muslim, 9 per cent Serbian, and the rest are none of the above. However, because municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina were created similarly as in Croatia, by composing Serbian and Bosnian population -- excuse me, Serbian and Muslim population in the territory of Croatia, or vice versa, by cleansing border areas, practically border areas of Herceg-Bosna, this creates approximately 65 per cent of the Croatian population in Herceg-Bosna. As if to validate his point, Boban offered that by comparison, even the Serbs were only 63 per cent of the population in Serbia. Kljuic had already made it clear to Tudjman that he would not support this Greater Croatia; that if that was Tudjman's view or that was Tudjman's course, that Kljuic was out of it. Kljuic said: "I did not agree to that policy, and even before this, when we spoke privately in the president's house and this was not recorded, I said to him, 'Mr. President, you cannot get me to do this. There's little Boban who could hardly wait to do it, but I was ready to resign.'" It is an adjudicated fact that from at least November 1991 forward, quote: "There is no doubt that the Republic of Croatia and the HZ-HB were pursuing the same ultimate goals; namely, the incorporation of Croatian provinces of Bosnia and Herzegovina into a single Croatian state." Two important facets or characteristics of this programme, the Greater Croatia Banovina programme or project, one was what we called in the course of the trial the two-track policy, which, essentially, in so many words, means: Say one thing, do another. Tudjman, Boban, and others knew, of course, that they could not openly advocate Bosnia's destruction. It was not the internationally-popular or accepted thing to say in polite diplomatic circles. Tudjman, at the 27 December meeting, says: "Under the present circumstances, gentlemen, from the general Croatian standpoint, a demarcation of borders suits us better ... This is not the first time that we have talked like this, even in this circle." In other words, Among us boys. "For tactical reasons, we did not raise this possibility publicly, because we did not want to be the one to raise it, the issue of borders." Some years later, in his suspect interview, Jadranko Prlic confirmed exactly this two-track policy in his admitted statement. And you've seen this before, I'm not going to read it all again, but Prlic very clearly tells us there was a plan -- there was one plan described to the public and there was one plan created -- another plan created among themselves. In the middle of that paragraph: "However, between themselves, they created another plan ..." That's two-track. There's another important feature of this, and that is that historical circumstances, for whatever reason, put a huge political advantage on the Croat side of the table, in terms of perception and negotiations. Tudjman, Boban, and the others knew that they could count on Milosevic and the Serbs almost always taking, at least publicly, a more extreme position and would bear the onus, in the vernacular, someone might say, they would take the heat for dividing Bosnia or much of it, so that Tudjman, Boban, and others did not even need to openly advocate partition, as some describe it, economists, political scientist, they could ride on the Serbs' coat tails in making such statements as, Well, Bosnia is already divided anyway, or, A sovereign Bosnia doesn't exist anymore anyway, or, It's going to be divided anyway. They could hide behind Milosevic and his coat tails. And here, again, Tudjman confirmed exactly that at the 27 December meeting: "The survival, the sovereignty of Bosnia in the present circumstances from the Croatian standpoint, is such that not only do we not have to advocate it, we must not even raise the issue openly." I don't have a slide on that. Let me say that again: "The survival, the sovereignty of Bosnia in the present circumstances from the Croatian standpoint, is such that not only do we not have to advocate it, we must not even raise the issue openly." Your Honours, that brings us to a point in the Prosecution's opening statement -- or, excuse me, closing argument where we will -- we would like to propose or we will present a video that is Exhibit P07437 on Greater Croatia. It is 40 minutes. We are going to -- after looking at it several times, we are going to play the whole thing, because based on everything that the Prosecution said up until now, we think that the Chamber will find the video a quite helpful final overview on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Reporter: On 'Dispatches' tonight, the unreported story of the Bosnian war, how the Croatian government has shared in the carve-up of Bosnia just as it always intended, and how it's got away with it. Tonight, as the Croats meet to talk peace with their former Muslim allies in Vienna, 'Dispatches' reveals the secret protocols that betrayed those same Muslims. That's 'Dispatches: How the Croats have Created a Brand-New country in Bosnia Just for Themselves and How the West has Turned a Blind Eye to a Greater Croatia.' "Capljina, a town in Herceg-Bosna, a new country few people have ever heard of, but a country that's determined to put itself on the European map. Herceg-Bosna is the mini-state that Croats have carved out of what was once Bosnia, and now Capljina's mayor, Pero Markovic, can look forward to a brave new world.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "In the future, I hope that with the help of the world and all those who have experience with life in democracy, we will be able to continue to live as others, the same way as Europe, because we are part of Europe. So we need to work. We must rebuild that which has been destroyed. We must go to school and get ready for life in Europe, to which we belong. "Reporter: But before Herceg-Bosna can take its place in Europe, towns like Capljina have a lot of work to do. Not just repairing the damage caused by the Serb attack 18 months ago, but also removing the traces of a second, more chilling battle. "Capljina seems to be getting back to normal, but scratch beneath the surface and everything has changed. One in four of the town's population has left. They didn't choose to go. "Six months ago, Capljina was sealed off by the militia. Street by street, block by block, a quarter of the town's people were loaded into buses and driven away. They were all Muslims. This was the final step in a campaign of persecution, which began when Muslim cafes and shops were looted and destroyed. "Herceg-Bosna has not emerged by accident. The setting up of this state is the realisation of a long-term plan. "Today, all the players in the Capljina football team are Croats. They play beneath the Croatian checker-board flag. The story of how the Serbs carved out their chunk of Bosnia is well known. The Croats have now done the same, but their game plan has been overlooked. "Herceg-Bosna owes its existence to one man, Croatian President Franjo Tudjman. For him, the making of a Croat state on Bosnian land has been a personal obsession, an obsession which drove him to bang the final nail into Bosnia's coffin. Tudjman has built this state on concentration camps, ethnic cleansing, torture, starvation, all executed by his henchman, Mate Boban."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Bosnia-Herzegovina will be an equal part -- be a state of the Croatian people, and the Croatian people will be its own master there." "Reporter: The Croats were the smallest group in Bosnia, fewer than a fifth of the population, but they've always dominated the baron landscape of Herzegovina. Herzegovinian's look to the Croatian capital, Zagreb, rather than Sarajevo as their capital. This rocky terrain bred the fascist Ustashas of World War II. To this day, Herzegovinians display a virulent strain of Croatian nationalism." "It is a philosophy of intolerance, a lot of prejudice, they hate the state as an institution, they hate taxes, they hate everything. They need only space and territory." "Reporter: After World War II, poverty drove tens of thousands of Herzegovinians to abandon this infertile land. In emigre communities abroad, their nationalist fervor only deepened. They dreamed of their region becoming part of Croatia. It was a dream shared by Croatian president Franjo Tudjman. He always believed that Croatia had a historic claim in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Bosnia-Herzegovina is an entity that came into being due to the Ottoman invasion of Europe. By that time -- or until that time, Bosnia was part of the Croatian state or there was a Bosnian kingdom, but it was Catholic, and it was linked with Croatia." "Reporter: Tudjman's obsession with Croatian claims in Bosnia runs deep. In 1991, he meets his arch enemy, Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, for secret discussions. Even though Serbia is threatening to invade Croatia, Tudjman is still happy to talk about their one common interest, a carve-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Two eye-witnesses of this meeting at Karadjordjevo can now reveal the real agenda.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Nowhere in the mass media has complete information about that been published. Those were secret talks, but they were given the appearance in the mass media as talks between Croatia and Serbia, about problems between these two countries, and no more than that. What's more, all rumours -- all talk that they were talking about Bosnia there were officially denied." "There were several maps on a table, I guess, and the idea was more or less close to the recent ideas on Bosnia-Herzegovina. That means, either to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina into 10 or 15 units or in 3 semi-independent states." "Reporter: Did the Muslims attend this meeting?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "No, absolutely not. Not a single representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina took part in the talks in Karadjordjevo or after Karadjordjevo. Those were bilateral talks between Serbian and Croatian representatives, but never were they attended by any representative of the Bosnian Muslims." "Reporter: Tudjman had swept to power on a nationalist ticket, but most of his advisers opposed his ambitions in Bosnia. However, Tudjman is an autocrat who listens only to the people who agree with him. "He found unconditional support elsewhere. Emigre Herzegovinians had poured money into Tudjman's election campaign. They were confident he would promote their nationalist ambitions not only in Croatia, but also in Bosnia. The most prominent is Gojko Susak. "Until four years ago, Susak was a pizza parlour entrepreneur in Toronto. Now he's the defence minister of Croatia." "The president had a view on Bosnia and Herzegovina long before we met. He was very explicit in that at the very first public speech when he came to the US and Canada. That's when I first met him. Politics in Bosnia-Herzegovina were defined. They do coincide with my view of Bosnia and Herzegovina in many ways, though." "There is a double game between the two. At personal level, Mr. Susak is a kind of Tudjman's slave. He accepts every decision that's made by Mr. Tudjman, so his non-existing personality, at personal level. But in political sense, Mr. Tudjman sometime or even at the present time very often exhibits political -- Mr. Susak's political philosophy." "Reporter: But for the Croats of Sarajevo and the rest of Bosnia, Tudjman's ambitions were dangerous. The Herzegovinians, who numbered 200.000, had always lived together, but 600.000 other Croats were scattered in mixed communities throughout Bosnia. They couldn't easily be disentangled. These Croats already had their own leadership in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "So that I won the election at the only legal convention of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina unanimously. I got a term in office for two years. After that, I often talked to President Tudjman, and I was always saying to him, 'You are the president of all Croats, but I am president of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina.' "Reporter: But unknown to Kljuic, the president of all Croats was already preparing the ground for a division of Bosnia. Even as he makes his first presidential visit to the Croats of Sarajevo, Tudjman is secretly backing a small group of extremist Herzegovina politicians who are plotting a separate Croat state in Bosnia. But he reveals nothing of his true intentions to this audience."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Ladies and gentlemen, in the past three years I have travelled the world a lot, but this meeting with you is certainly the most touching." "Reporter: 'Dispatches' has obtained the signed secret protocol produced by that group in November 1991. It confirms decisions reached with Tudjman in Zagreb. It declares Croatian people within Bosnia-Herzegovina must finally start a decisive and active policy which is supposed to lead us to our centuries-long dream, a common Croatian state. They'll show Europe and the world which regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina are Croatian and where our future lies. "The document lays out the real plan. First, a Croat province in Bosnia is declared. Next, any Croat leaders who support a united Bosnia must be removed. Within two months of the meeting, with Tudjman's backing, the separatists force Kljuic to resign. Herzegovinian Mate Boban, whose main claim to fame was the spell in jail for black marketeering, is installed as the new leader. The plan is underway. Boban moves the Croat power base to this factory to his hometown of Grude, in Herzegovina. This town, with just two main streets and no town square, takes the place of a sophisticated Sarajevo. The next stage is simple. Boban sets up a separate Croat army in Bosnia, the HVO. "March 1992, Croats vote with Muslims for independence. The Serbs rebel, and war breaks out. "As the Serbs cut a swath through Bosnia, the Croatia steps in to help the beleaguered state. Tudjman signs a military alliance with Bosnian President Izetbegovic to fight the Serbs. Tudjman knows that the mainly Muslim Bosnian government has little choice but to rely on Croatia. This serves his purpose."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Initially, the Muslims were not prepared to fight the Serbian aggression, and then they accepted the agreement on the joint fight of the Croats and Muslims against the Serb aggression." "We thought that Muslims would join Croatia. That was -- I mean, that was a second thought behind his political mind." "Reporter: Croats and Muslims link up to fight the Serbs. Many Muslims join the HVO, which is better prepared than government forces."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I was with the HVO. I was even platoon commander. And somehow I expected that the alliance would hold." "Reporter: Once the alliances halted the Serb alliance, Boban moves to the next stage of the master plan. He declares that the Bosnian government is dissolved and announces that the HVO has taken over in all areas unoccupied by the Serbs. The strains in the alliance are obvious." "Well, superficially, they were working together as partners. There was a coalition which had taken them through the referendum on independence, and, on the face of it, you thought that you were dealing with the Croats and the Muslims versus the Serbs. It was not many weeks before I realised that this was not a true coalition."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And then without the Muslim participation, we were able to defend 35 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina against a Serb aggressor. In those areas, because there were no more authorities, Bosnia-Herzegovina had disappeared, we established the Croatian Defence Council as a temporary government in the free areas to protect the people and their property, and to establish the basic functions in these areas, such as education, health-care, and so on."
