"Reporter: But to the HVO's supposed partner in the alliance, the take-over seems far from temporary. Ivan Negovetic is a Croat who enlisted not in the HVO, but in the Bosnian Government army."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "HVO takes over power. They take the police station in the municipality, they appoint their own officials, and they remove all elements of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which means our flag, other symbols, everything that makes up the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and proclaim a new state." "Reporter: To tighten its grip across Bosnia, the HVO has to weaken its alliance partner. 'Dispatches' has obtained official documents which show the restrictions the HVO placed on the Bosnian Army. In many areas supposedly under joint control, the HVO requisitions all industry, power supplies, and transport. All consignments of weapons to the Bosnian Army need to pass through Croatia and Herzegovina. At each check-point, some of the consignment is hived off, and most of the weapons end up in HVO hands. In Grude alone, 37 trucks of weapons intended for the defence of Sarajevo are halted and plundered."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And we tolerated that. We even tolerated the fact that they sell back the weapons that they had plundered from us, although these weapons had already been paid by our people in foreign countries. But we didn't want to open another front. We tried to avoid another conflict. But then logistical supply routes had completely been cut off, and then we didn't receive even 15 per cent." "Reporter: In some areas, Bosnian forces are disarmed and expelled by the Croats. In others, they fight back and push the HVO out. "Serb aggression becomes a distant memory, as Croats and Muslims begin a scramble for territory. They fight each other with the bitterness born of betrayal. Bosnia is dead."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The Bosnian crisis by this appears in a totally new light, not as a fascist aggression of Serbian Montenegro against an independent state, but the atmosphere of civil war is created in which everybody shoots at each other."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "While the Muslims and Croats were still together, you could still talk about Bosnia. But when the Croatian-Muslim conflict broke out, then the Muslim policy also had to change. Certainly, the idea of a unified Bosnia was destroyed with the Croatian attack against the Muslims." "Reporter: Tudjman and Boban are already rewriting history. They planned to seize power across Bosnia, but the Bosnian Army stopped them. Now the official Croat line blames Muslims for destroying the alliance."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Apart from that, we Croats are really guilty of what's happening, because with good intentions, we helped the Muslims, who were victims of Serb aggression, we helped them to stay alive and helped them regain their dignity in every respect, and above all we gave them the means to kill Croats."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The extremist elements prevailed, and they were growing stronger, so the Muslims opted for a long war against the Croats instead of a political solution. They opted for a long war itself a political solution." "Reporter: As the alliance crumbled, Western negotiators failed to react to the Croats' territorial ambitions. The Croats had taken care to pose as the reasonable party in the Bosnian conflict." "They were the weakest group because they're the smallest group, and I think they were quite clever, politically, to decide that, by and large, they would go along with the negotiators. They would be the reasonable party. That was in their interests to be that, and I think that was a clever strategy." "Reporter: That strategy is about to pay dividends. Now the peace negotiators are poised to give the Croats a green light for the final dismantling of Bosnia. "December 1992, Geneva. As the Vance-Owen Peace Plan is being drafted, the Croats are tightening their grip throughout their planned mini-state, Herceg-Bosna. The plan divides Bosnia into 10 provinces, but it appears to ignore Mate Boban's obvious territorial ambitions, ambitions which the negotiators knew only too well." "One was well aware that they had been pursuing their own agenda way before the Vance-Owen Plan was announced; that is, we were very conscious of it. The Herceg-Bosna question was a constant issue between President Izetbegovic and President Tudjman, so, you know, it was nothing -- there were no surprises by then. We were fully aware of what was their private agenda." "Reporter: Even so, the Croats see the Vance-Owen Peace Plan as an endorsement of their private agenda. Two of the provinces have a clear Croat majority. A third is half Muslim. Boban claims this province for himself. He insists that Vance-Owen has rewarded Croats with over a quarter of Bosnia. He hurries to sign."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The Vance-Owen Plan was one of the best possible options for the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is a pity that it wasn't understood either by Europe or by the US, the UN, the Serbs, and the Muslims." "Reporter: The Vance-Owen Plan places Mostar the mixed city of Mostar in a Croat province. The Croats have long coveted Mostar as their capital. They use the peace plan as a green light for a take-over. But Vance-Owen also binds each province to protect ethnic minorities. The Croats appear not to notice."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "After they signed the Vance-Owen Plan, the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina thought that the division was accomplished. We got our Herceg-Bosna as our para-state, and we can do whatever we want. We can rename the streets, we can rename the Croatian universities. And Mostar was finally the capital of our newly-created state. And they thought that it was a fait accompli, but they were wrong." "Reporter: May 9th, 1993. The Croats mount an all-out assault on Mostar. The Bosnian forces resist. "Have you always seen Mostar as the capital of Herceg-Bosna?" "Yes, all the time." "Reporter: Even though it was a majority Muslim?" "No, there were no majority Muslim, of any nation. Before the war, the equal number of inhabitants were Muslims and Croats. The difference was only a few hundred." "Reporter: But still you saw it as the capital of the Croatian part of Bosnia and Herzegovina?" "Yes. Yes, it is. "Reporter: Why?" "Because this republic must have a capital, must have one centre, must have university, must have other things which makes the republic a republic on one civilisation level, the theatre, the symphonic orchestra, and so on." "Reporter: But that civilised capital does not include Muslims. All the Muslims living on the west side are rounded up and forced across the river to the devastated east side. A brutal siege begins. Civilians become a weapon of war."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I used to live on the right bank. We had a lovely two-bedroom apartment which was fully furnished. We had both worked for 25 years. Everything is still there. They drove us out. We were used as human shields. We weren't allowed to take anything with us." "Reporter: I saw a film where there was a night-shot of people being driven out of West Mostar into East Mostar by HVO troops? [Voiceover] "... not much could have been recorded even in Somalia." "Reporter: For four months the HVO blocks all relief convoys to Muslim-held East Mostar. As the battle for the capital of Herceg-Bosna grinds on, Boban continues to starve civilians there. He is still using food as a weapon in his war."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "First thing in the morning, you have to fight for fuel wood. You have to go around to the destroyed houses to try and get some fuel wood. Although much of it has already been taken, people need it. And after that, you try to get some water for cooking, and if you have anything to put in a pot, you cook. That's what you do. It's very difficult, to be honest. And then if there's shelling, you go and see if your family are still alive. Every morning, we count heads to see who was killed and who wasn't, who has been wounded and who's still okay. And food, oh, my God, if you manage to eat, you eat once a day; sometimes twice, but that happens only rarely." "Reporter: Across the river on the Croatian-held side of Mostar, there's no shortage of food." "Mostar don't have west bank, don't have east bank. Mostar is a beautiful town, and I don't recognise this division. It's temporary front-line, but I am inhabitant of Mostar, Mostar is my native town, and I don't want to divide it." "Reporter: Other natives of West Mostar are busy sweeping away the last traces of their neighbours. 'Dispatches' found some photographs among the ashes."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is a shame to throw away anything. I found my neighbour's photograph albums. I took them. Everything that I found in rubbish, I put them in 50-kilo bags. If they ever return, I want to give it to them. If this peace ever came back, we'll give them back their memories."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Most of them are on the east bank or living abroad." "Reporter: The Croats steadily work their way through the order of war pioneered by the Bosnian Serbs. In the Mostar region, Muslim men of fighting age are herded off to camps, such as Dretelj. Many had fought in the HVO."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Dretelj is hell on earth. It's a place where a Croat could kill a Muslim and not be held responsible for that. People were systematically destroyed there. There was no food, no water, no sanitation. Health-care was virtually non-existent. People were tortured every day. They were ill treated every day. Many people died." "Reporter: On an island just off the Croatian mainland, Muslim victims from Dretelj Detention Camp are still held under police guard. 'Dispatches' filmed there secretly." "It's important for you at the moment ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "For the time being, you have to go somewhere where you will be safe, because your refugee status has been extended by only a month." "Reporter: The government of Herceg-Bosna released these men only on condition that they would be sent abroad by the United Nations. They have left Bosnia forever." "It's important that you secure your safety."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Croatia had to release us from Dretelj to clear its name, but as you can see, we were not sent home to Bosnia. We were sent to Croatia, and we can only stay there temporarily until we're sent to third countries. It's just another stage in the process of ethnic cleansing." "Reporter: Throughout the war against Bosnian government forces, the regular Croatian Army continues to pour into Bosnia to reinforce the HVO. This Croatian soldier was photographed on the front-line in Mostar last June."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Before the conflict, the HVO didn't have a single tank. Now they have scores of tanks in the area, so it's clear that they got help either from Croatia or through Croatia. And we have also recorded conversations. We can tell from the soldiers' accents that they come from the regular Croatian Army." "Reporter: We have evidence of Croat Army tanks in Buski.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We also have evidence of your own British tanks in Pakistan and in India." "There is, and as I speak, very substantial elements of the Croatian Army in Bosnia and Herzegovina, very substantial, and I must say I think it's an issue which the world ought to address more strongly. They addressed it in terms of the Serbs in the spring of 1992 with various considerable strength of purpose. They have, to a great extent, ignored it in the last six months as it's built up." "Reporter: President Tudjman's ambitions in Bosnia have been so ignored, but in the Croatian capital of Zagreb, it's business as usual. Croatia's backing of atrocities in Bosnia has gone unpunished. A senior diplomat told 'Dispatches' the Croats have got away with murder, literally. At a European Community meeting in July, ministers rejected sanctions." "Certainly, that is the view of the European Community, obliviously influenced by the Federal Republic of Germany and other friends of Croatia like Austria and the United Nations, Hungary and others, and the United States. So the general feeling has been that it is better to make representations to President Tudjman and to criticise and to argue, rather than to take action in terms of sanctions against Croat." "We need an appropriate international approach to the Balkans, and until present time we have experienced many strange international politicians, genuinely losers in their own countries, like Lord Owen, Lord Carrington, Lord that and that, and they were sent to this part of the earth to play irresponsible political games." "Reporter: One winner in these irresponsible political games has been Franjo Tudjman. In July, he abandoned any pretence of supporting a unified Bosnia by calling openly for a carve-up. Peace negotiations are now based on a union of republics or mini-states. Tudjman has satisfied his obsession. Next on the agenda, the joining of this part of Bosnia with Croatia."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I believe that we will become part of Croatia. That is the goal of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Croats in Herzegovina and in Bosnia are the same. The Croats in Herzegovina are an undivided part of the Croatian nation."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We need to be aware of how important a moment is in the history of a nation and peoples. Croatia's borders in the past and now, and not just the borders of Croatia. Unfortunately, we are at the crossroads of civilisations. "Reporter: In Herceg-Bosna, in towns like Capljina, the new state is taking shape. The few factories are getting back to work. Children are getting used to a new curriculum, the same one taught in the Croatian motherland. "But just outside Capljina, a convoy waits to collect the Croat refugees driven out from central Bosnia. For these people, Tudjman and Boban's land grab has backfired. They come from outside Herceg-Bosna, where the HVO is losing more and more territory to Bosnian government forces. The Croats of Central Bosnia are now reduced to a few besieged pockets, falling one by one. The latest is Vares, where 20.000 people have fled. Mate Boban's only solution is to offer them a home in the barren land of Herceg-Bosna. "In Sarajevo, Croats face an uncertain future. Thirty-thousand Croats live here. It's still the largest Croat city in Bosnia, but the Herceg-Bosna government has abandoned them. Only the church is left to protect them. "The spiritual leader of all Croats in Bosnia, Archbishop Vinko Puljic, refuses to leave his cathedral, despite constant pressure to move to Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "From the 27th of December, 1992, the Croats have had no officially-elected representatives in the parliament. They are outside of Sarajevo. And since then, we have been living in suspense." "Reporter: Ivan Tomislav is a Croat citizen of Sarajevo. He feels betrayed by Mate Boban and his fellow Herzegovinians in Grude."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "What they're doing over there, the politicians in Grude, they just implement policies that are being dictated in Zagreb, and their policies do not represent the interests of all Croats from the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was never consulted about these political solutions. I never voted for them. Herceg-Bosna is not a solution, it's not an integral solution for all the Croats and Catholics in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, I cannot approve a unilateral political solution unless that political solution protects all of my believers. I demand a political solution that protects the rights of all of my believers." "Reporter: For the Croats in Sarajevo, Mate Boban's invitation to come and join other Croats in Herceg-Bosna is unacceptable."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I'd like to thank Mr. Boban for his proposal, but I could never live in Mostar or in Grude. I don't know where. I feel at home here in Sarajevo despite the shells. The living conditions are almost non-existent, but we will survive." "This is a tragedy, and this tragedy could be attributed to the leadership of Mr. Tudjman, because he has made many wrong decisions and, I mean, he -- he's simply -- I mean, his mentality is a mentality of a genuine loser."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "They are blind. They are politically a blind man, and they want to sacrifice 700.000 Croats from the whole of Bosnia for 170.000 Croats in Herzegovina." "Reporter: The choice now facing Bosnian Croats is stark. For most, it's Herceg-Bosna or nothing. President Tudjman has carved out his chunk of rock in Bosnia. He's fulfilled his personal obsession with no international reprisals, but the price has been the betrayal of Bosnia and the sacrifice of his own people."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The place where I left off in the chronology, Your Honours, before the video was at the end of December 1991, at the 27 December 1991 meeting. I would just refer to a couple of things in the video. The Prosecution submits that one of the reference documents about the so-called road map or plan that was referenced was the record of the meeting on the 12th of November, 1991, which is P00071, which was already referred to earlier in my comments, and we believe that the -- we submit that the reference -- the so-called partnership agreement between Bosnia and Croatia was the so-called friendship agreement in July of 1992, just if those references might assist the Chamber. I apologise for my health and my voice. I'm sorry for that, Your Honours. There are a lot of important events that happened in the first six months of 1992. There's the Livno meeting, which is important; there's the referendum that's been referred to now several times in the video; there are additional meetings and communications with and involving Mr. Tudjman and others, President Tudjman and others; there is the declared independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a new state; there is the formation of the new BiH state armed forces. During that time-period, the Herceg-Bosnians established the HVO military in April 1992, at the same time calling the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina illegal and the enemy. Petkovic, Praljak, and others are active during this time with the active support of the state of Croatia in establishing the HVO military and getting things moving. Largely because of the time element, however, I'm going to generally go past those events so that I can get more quickly to the second half of 1992, starting approximately July. In doing so, I just want to make clear that I'm not minimising or dismissing for a moment the importance of some of these other items, but we simply have to make some selections in what we're able to cover. The Chamber will recall other evidence in the case, perhaps other evidence from our pre-trial brief, from our final brief, other submissions that have been made that may assist the Chamber in that regard. Before we go to July, however, I do want to pause on the topic of what we've called Croatisation or persecution, just so that point is clear. By April 1992 and thereafter, at the same time that Herceg-Bosna was asserting its political, territorial, and ethnic sovereignty and separation by rejecting the BiH government, declaring the BiH armed forces illegal and, instead, establishing its own HVO and its own HVO government, the Herceg-Bosna HVO leaders were also pursuing a deliberate and sustained programme of persecution, Croatisation, and discrimination against Muslims and other non-Croats. Indeed, the seizure of 30 municipalities by the Herceg-Bosna leadership in a gathering composed only of Croats, with only 12 of those municipalities even having a Croat-majority population, with no vote, no consent, no agreement with the Muslims, was, itself, a persecutory and discriminatory act. The fundamental fact that virtually all government and military names were Croatian this and Croatian that, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council, the Croatian Post Office, the Croatian University of Mostar, made it very clear that this was a new territory for one ethnic group. The Prosecution position is that Herceg-Bosna's seizure of power and the process of Croatisation starting in the spring of 1992 is part of the persecution charged in the indictment. This extends back well into the spring, as we've just said, the spring of 1992. Some people might refer to that as softer forms of persecution, but, nonetheless, part of the persecution charged in the indictment. Every effort was made to make virtually everything in Herceg-Bosna Croatian, from state symbols and insignia, to language, educational curriculum, currency, place names; for example, Prozor -- with Prozor changing its name to Rama and Gornji Vakuf being changed to Skopje. In short, Herceg-Bosna was supposed to look, feel, and sound like Croatia; remember, top-down, territory, demographics, Croat-ness. A particular dark side of Croatisation was the official use or encouragement of Ustasha names and symbols, many associated with notorious World War II criminals, like as Ante Pavelic, Jure Francetic, and Rafael Boban. A section of the street formerly named after Mostar author Aleksa Santic was renamed in honour of the Ustasha leader, Dr. Mile Budak. And another street was named after two other leaders of the wartime independent state of Croatia, Vokic and Lorkovic, which was understandably quite offensive to non-Croats and, I take it, probably quite offensive to many Croats as well. An HVO brigade, the one Your Honours watched taking the oath, I asked Your Honours to draw back on your memories of when we saw the video of this oath-taking ceremony, the name of that unit was the Jure Francetic Brigade, a notorious World War II Ustasha war criminal. We will eventually come to discuss such things as command climate, and we ask the judges what sort of command climate -- what kind of message does it send when you name your military units after notorious war criminals. Here's a further important point, we submit, before moving ahead to July, but about talking now about the Croatisation. It again has been a consistent Defence theme or claim that Herceg-Bosna was something only temporary, only to take the temporary place of these allegedly non-functioning BiH authorities. If that was true, if that was true, these temporary -- these so-called temporary substitute Herceg-Bosna authorities could certainly have continued using the BiH flag and symbols, they could have applied BiH law, they could have used the existing names of BiH authorities and places, they could have used ethnic-neutral terms. Why did everything have to be Croatian? Why all the talk about Croatian territory? Why all the talk about, This is Croatian land? If it was a temporary, stand-in government, only temporarily for the benefit of the so-called non-functioning BiH government, why did you need Croatisation? In fact, wouldn't it have been more multi-ethnic -- wouldn't a more multi-ethnic -- a more ethnic neutral approach been less hostile and less provocative and less persecutory towards the Muslims? By 1995, Jadranko Prlic proudly reported to Tudjman: "Mr. President, people are being born and dying with the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It is both their birth and death certificate and the flag under which they are buried. That has infiltrated all the people's pores down there. Therefore, people are both emotionally and profoundly connected to this." Now, moving to July, approximately. By this time, as I said a few moments ago, an awful lot of things have happened that are important to the case. The HVO military is up and running. They have rejected completely the BiH authorities, the BiH armed forces, again, calling them illegal and, quote, "the enemy." That pattern of behaviour, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits, is exactly that. The pattern that the Chamber will see once again, not only in 1992, but in January of 1993 and April 1993 and throughout 1993; that is, this: Once the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership had determined a particular course of action or saw an opportunity to expand or consolidate its power, it took such action or grabbed such power or territory, even if other relevant parties had not, in fact, agreed or consented to such action or even opposed it. The HVO would go forward based on its own view or interpretation of events, seizing power or territory or, as some might say, jumping the gun, where there was no valid basis or consent that it do so. The continuing direct and high-level involvement of persons such as Milivoj Petkovic and Bruno Stojic can be seen in connection with several events in late June and early July 1992. Petkovic plainly confirms the HVO's widespread and systematic programme to take control of the, quote, "Croatian municipalities" and, quote, "Croatian territory "in his report to a Herceg-Bosna leadership gathering on the 26th of June, 1992. It can only have been with great pride that Petkovic reported his accomplishments and described his programme, which he set out as four main tasks: "Through offensive activities in the entire area of South-east Herzegovina, HVO forces, with assistance of considerable HV forces and equipment, have achieved success ..." "Today, we have under control almost the entire territory of Croatian municipalities (Neum, Ravno, Stolac, Capljina, Ljubuski, Citluk, Siroki Brijeg, and Mostar." "Admittedly, there is still part of the territory, mostly in Mostar and Stolac municipalities, that are not under control of HVO forces. "Therefore, we have four main tasks in front of us: "1. To put under control the remaining area of Croatian municipalities; "2. To secure and fortify the achieved line; "3. To carry out re-organising of the existing HVO forces; and "4. To establish Croatian rule over all municipalities. "Our intentions are: To prepare ourselves and through offensive activities liberate the remaining Croatian territory." Notwithstanding the pace at which they had moved the Herceg-Bosna programme forward or, indeed, because of that rapid pace, by early July 1992, Tudjman and his Herceg-Bosna cohorts were confronted with two major problems: First, the Republic of Croatia was under increasing international pressure because of its direct intervention and interference in a sovereign UN member state of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and, second, the resistance and opposition of the internationally-recognised BiH authorities, and Muslims generally, to the Herceg-Bosna para-state were becoming louder and stronger. By the 15th of May, 1992, Croatia was already being condemned for its actions in BiH. In Resolution 752, the UN Security Council condemned, quote, "all forms of interference from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, including by elements of the Croatian Army," and demanded that such elements, quote, "now in Bosnia and Herzegovina," quote, "either be withdrawn or be subject to the authority of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or be disbanded and disarmed." The same resolution also demanded that all irregular forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina be disbanded and disarmed with this description including the HVO as a paramilitary force, which up to this point in time had steadfastly refused to put itself under BiH state control. The Secretary-General reported to the Security Council two weeks later, on 30 May 1992, that: "As regards the withdrawal of elements of the Croatian Army now in Bosnia and Herzegovina, information currently available in New York suggests that no such withdrawal has occurred." This report was followed by new Security Council Resolution 757 on 30 May 1992. "... deploring the fact that the demands of Resolution 752 have not been complied with, including its demands that Bosnia-Herzegovina's neighbours take swift action to end all interference and respect the territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina." In this context, and illustrating again the operation of the two-track policy, the Croatian leadership affirmed its recognition and support for the BiH state government and its efforts to establish a single unified armed forces under the BiH Presidency's command. Note: The very BiH government whose armed forces and commanders, the orders of which have been called and labelled by the Herceg-Bosnans as illegal and invalid. Zagreb says, We support you with UN forces. Don't worry, Izetbegovic, we're right behind you. At the same time, our Herceg-Bosna clients are telling you to stay out of Herceg-Bosna, it's none of your business, your forces are illegal and your orders invalid. That's two-track. We can see that in a letter -- in a joint statement issued by Tudjman and Izetbegovic on the 12th of June 1992. In item number 3: "The Republic of Croatia supports the efforts of Bosnia and Herzegovina to maintain its independence and resist aggression, and to this end offers and will continue to offer its help. The Republic of Croatia also supports the efforts of the legal government and Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina to consolidate the defence of the republic by uniting all forms and components of armed defence to the unified armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the superior command of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Of course, if Herceg-Bosna and the HVO were, in fact, in any way a genuine and legitimate part of BiH, or wanted to be, they would have joined and could have been subject to the legal governmental authorities and the single unified state command. Clearly, they had no desire to do so. Tudjman, Boban, and the others must have hoped that this joint statement, signed by Izetbegovic and Tudjman on the 12th of June, 1992, they must have hoped that that would answer or assuage the Muslims' increasingly vocal opposition to Herceg-Bosna. This opposition is illustrated in a platform for the activities of the president of BiH in state of war issued by the BiH Presidency on 26th June 1992. I'm going to try to save a few moments of time by paraphrasing, and simply this is yet one more in a series of statements which BiH authorities flatly rejected Herceg-Bosna para-states and parallel institutions in Bosnia. I'll refer to one quote out of several. The platform stated that BiH would, quote, "not accept negotiations which have as their basis the establishment of ethnically-pure territories or a regional division of Bosnia and Herzegovina on a solely ethnic basis." Despite this clearly stated opposition, Tudjman and others were determined to push forward with Herceg-Bosna. On the 5th of July 1992, Tudjman, Susak, the Croat hard-liner Vice Vukojevic, and others met with Boban and several Bosnian Croat leaders, including Milenko Brkic. Now, a reminder about Mr. Brkic. Following the major fall-out -- the falling out between Boban and the HDZ party president Kljuic, Kljuic has kind of half-resigned. He was not formally -- I don't know, maybe he was just being difficult. He would not officially completely withdraw, but he took on an inactive role. And in his place, as the acting president of the party, this Milenko Brkic had been put in that position. As time will tell, and as we'll get to it in the next few moments, unfortunately Mr. Brkic suffered the same predicament of as Mr. Kljuic, because he proved to be far too moderate for Boban, Boras, Kordic, and the others. In a meeting reminiscent of the 27 September 1991 show-down between Boban and Kljuic, the HDZ BiH party president Brkic and others, much to Tudjman's and Boban's consternation, raised serious questions about Herceg-Bosna, saying that it was not right for the HVO to take power from the legitimate BiH authorities and that the Muslims were not accepting this, especially in areas where the Muslims were in the majority. Mr. Brkic says, and this is from one of the presidential transcripts: "Many people are asking if the work of the HDZ BiH party has been suspended or not. The question is whether a party convention should be held or not. What is Herceg-Bosna, what kind of association is it, and Posavina and Central Bosnia also need to be clarified. What is their relationship with the state, as a whole? What is the HVO? Is this an army or a civilian structure, and what is the scope of its authority? This has not been clarified sufficiently. The HVO has suspended regular civilian authority and even the HDZ party. "There has been much recklessness in work. The question arises of who should be obeyed in the future, who is authorised to replace people, which are the legally-elected organs of authority, and so forth? "Relations with Muslims are growing complicated. The HDZ party has adopted conclusions and paid tribute to the HVO for what it has done so far, especially regarding free territories. However, the HDZ does not agree with the suspension of civilian authority." As you read those and look at those words, this is the president of the HDZ-Bi -- the acting president, Bosnian Croat president of the HDZ-BiH, saying, We don't really know. What is Herceg-Bosna, what is the HVO? What's going on here? Brkic continued, indicating that people from Zagreb were playing in these matters, and, quote, "I doubt their good intentions." Mr. Maric from Grude explains many of the things he implements by saying he has been in contact with Mr. Tudjman who backs these positions, et cetera." Boban roughly dismissed Brkic's statements, despite the fact that, at least on paper, Brkic was his superior, his party leader. Boban: "If I had known that these would be the participants in the meeting and that we would have this kind of discussion, it is certain that I would not have come, because I have far more pressing business." I said to you earlier that one of the transcripts or documents the Chamber should look at would be the 27 December meeting. I also highly recommend to the Chamber the record of the meeting with Brkic and others on the 5th of July, 1992, which I believe is P00312, another highly-telling meeting. Boban's reaction and his anger and frustration with Brkic really leap off the page, and he says, as he says here: "If I had known that we were going to be talking about this, I wouldn't have even come." It is clear that the policy being conducted now -- Tudjman then comes in -- I'm sorry. Tudjman then comes into the conversation, same meeting: "It is clear that the policy being conducted now cannot satisfy everyone in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The HDZ leadership must remain consistent in conducting a unified policy. "It is up to you to assess whether a HDZ convention should be held or not. "The main problem of cantonisation and the relations towards the Muslims, and the role of the authorities in and the HVO ... in building up a government and what is being recommended and advocated by Mr. Izetbegovic, one must be very careful, because his deeds are something else. Let us not delude ourselves with certain promises. The essential thing is that we must not lose our Croatian identity. We have to have our territories, which have been Croatian territories throughout history, especially those where the Croats have lived as a majority for years." Tudjman had no trouble recognising and stating plainly that the HVO had, indeed, established a, quote, "new government," and expressly rejecting the single multi-ethnic BiH that moderate Croats, like Kljuic and Jerko Doko, who was then the BiH defence minister, were advocating. The HVO deserves credit -- this is Tudjman: "The HVO deserves credit for the establishment of a new government and new relations. The system of authority being created by Kljuic and Doko is not for us. For us, the core of authority must lie in the HDZ ... "We have to organise military and civilian authority within the framework of the Community of Herceg-Bosna." Brkic then comes back at Tudjman and says: "There's a fundamental inconsistency in your position. You cannot, on the one hand, say that you recognise the sovereignty and independence of BiH, but not recognise its authorities." Brkic told Tudjman: "If you recognise BH, it is logical to recognise the government. Just how much that government can act and how functional it is at the moment is a separate matter. If this is just a declaration, then what is happening in practice? The government surely has a conception of how to resolve the problems." Like Boban, the Croat hard-liner Vukojevic, could hardly stomach the conversation: "It is certain that there are divisions in the HDZ along the Bosnian line. A division certainly exists, and one of them is Jure Pelivan's Sarajevo option, which I oppose." We'll get to Mr. Pelivan in the next meeting. He was at that time the Croat -- the Bosnian Croat prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Susak complained that Herceg-Bosna had not yet gone far enough: "We have managed to encircle the territories," we've drawn the lines on the map, we have territory, "but have not succeeded in accomplishing organs of power." As with Kljuic before him, it was clear from this meeting that Brkic's days in the HDZ leadership were numbered, with his moderate views plainly not acceptable to Boban, Vukojevic, and the hard-liners, and, indeed, by the fall of 1992, Brkic was replaced by Boban himself, as discussed below, soon we'll get there. A few days later, on the 21st of July, 1992, following the UN's protest in May concerning the Croatia's involvement in Bosnia, Tudjman met with Izetbegovic and others at an important meeting in Zagreb. This is Exhibit P00339, and I will add this to my list -- my short list of those transcripts that should be read in full. This Tudjman, Izetbegovic, Jure Pelivan, Brkic, all, if I can use an American term, duking it out, fighting each other, debating on the direction of things in Bosnia. And, again, add that to your short list of transcripts to read. Remember that -- we're coming up on a break, but if I can just -- remember at this time there are already two outstanding Security Council resolutions condemning Croatia's involvement in Bosnia. Tudjman's got a problem. He's got to somehow deal with that. He's either got to leave Bosnia, which by all indications he doesn't want to do, or he has to get some legitimacy or some cover for their presence there, and that leads us to this so-called friendship meeting with Izetbegovic on the 21st of July, 1992. Mr. President, I suggest that might be a time to stop for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have our last break, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Scott, the Trial Chamber is asking you to tell us the number of all these documents that you're quoting. I believe that so far you haven't forgotten any, but make sure that you always tell us what is the exact reference of the exhibit that you're quoting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will endeavour to do that, and maybe if I can just be so bold, if I miss some and if I fail, I'll be happy to assist the Chamber's staff following the argument, if that may also assist. But I will do my best. Sorry, I'm just -- I was just consulting with Ms. Winner about -- yes, sorry. We were talking, Your Honours -- my apologies. We were talking about the 21 July 1992 so-called friendship meeting. I mentioned before the break that one of -- excuse me, one of Tudjman's serious problems at the time was that he had the UN Security Council breathing down his neck about Croatia's involvement in Bosnia. The meeting transcript makes clear, the Prosecution submits, that Franjo Tudjman had three principle goals for this meeting: First, obtaining Izetbegovic's agreement for the Croatian Army's presence in BiH, thus solving his problem with the UN; number 2, getting Izetbegovic to accept the HVO military as a recognised part of the BiH armed forces; and, third, gaining Izetbegovic's acceptance of Herceg-Bosna as a governmental/territorial entity in space. The end of the meeting and the resulting written agreement, the so-called friendship agreement, showed that Tudjman was only partly successful as to one of the three goals, in gaining a qualified acceptance of the HVO military, but only on the same condition as the BiH Presidency had been saying since April, If you truly become one of us, if you truly become part of this army under a single unified command, then, indeed, you are welcome to join us. As to the other goals, Tudjman plainly failed. While the final friendship agreement concluded -- and the friendship agreement is P00339. While the final agreement included language about military co-operation against the Serbs on both sides of the Croatian-Bosnian border, there are no words in the agreement allowing HV presence in Bosnia. It may have given Croatia a bit of cover, but it was ultimately clear that Tudjman did not get the language that he wanted, as Tudjman, himself, later confirms. And I don't know if I'll run out of time or not, but I will tell the Chamber that as you read the presidential transcripts through the late summer and fall of 1992, what you see and read Tudjman saying over and over again, We didn't get it. We went there, we had the meeting in July. We didn't get the agreement we wanted. He says it over and over again. On Herceg-Bosna, the acceptance of Herceg-Bosna, Izetbegovic's answer to Tudjman's repeated requests that he accept Herceg-Bosna was a resounding, No, and probably no surprise at this point. Now, going back and touching with a bit more detail in terms of the HVO as a military force, while plainly rejecting Herceg-Bosna, Izetbegovic made it clear, and you can again see it from the transcript, that it would be acceptable and, indeed, even desirable for the HVO military to become a genuinely integrated part of the single BiH state armed forces under the command of the BiH Presidency. The Chamber may recall the Croatian witness Zuzul who came and testified during the Prlic Defence case, and he said that this was such an important meeting and, quote, "We measured our words carefully the whole day; not just paragraphs, but words ... this document was prepared," the friendship agreement, "... this document was prepared in a very, very serious manner." That being the case, Tudjman and the HVO could not have obtained what they were hoping for, since none of this, quote, "carefully measured words" indicate that the HVO would not be subordinate to the BiH Presidency as supreme commander or to a single ABiH command. Section 6 of the final agreement states: "The armed component of the Croatian Defence Council (that is, the HVO military) is an integral part of the united armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Croatian Defence Council will have its representatives in the joint command of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Among the carefully-measured words, there is nothing about the HVO being a separate but equal army, there's nothing about it having equal representation or power in a command system, there's nothing about the fact that it would control the command of the BiH state armed forces or that the HVO would somehow continue to exist somehow equal but somehow entirely separate under a separate command. There's no basis for those views in the friendship agreement signed by Izetbegovic and Tudjman. As to Herceg-Bosna, Izetbegovic couldn't have been clearer, rejecting Tudjman's repeated efforts to get him to accept it. He states at one point: "We do not agree with that item ... I think that the agreement shouldn't interfere in internal. Everything else is an internal issue of Bosnia and Herzegovina and will be regulated over there ... It could be a little bit scandalous if someone would ... say the constitutional order has been regulated in Zagreb." Tudjman tried to force the issue, but Izetbegovic steadfastly refused, except to recognise, quote, "full equality of the three constitutive peoples: Muslims, Croats and Serbs." Izetbegovic told Tudjman: "It is obviously the point about which we cannot agree because this is implicating some things that may cause secession tomorrow." Both the Bosnian Croat acting president of the HDZ-BiH, now we're back to Mr. Brkic and Mr. Pelivan - I told you we would come back to them in a moment - they are also in the same meeting. Both the Bosnian Croat acting president of the HDZ-BiH, Miljenko Brkic, and the Bosnian Croat prime minister of Bosnia, Jure Pelivan, agree in this meeting -- agree with Izetbegovic, that talking about the legitimacy of Herceg-Bosna was completely different than accepting the HVO military as part of the BiH armed forces if, indeed, and genuinely subordinated to a joint and single unified command. Brkic and Pelivan go on to say that Herceg-Bosna's actions in taking power would, if they had not already, lead to a, quote, "serious conflict with the Muslims." Brkic told Tudjman: "Mr. President, when the HVO appears as a military structure, then the Muslims and Croats are united, but at the moment when the HVO appears as a civilian structure, then the Muslims don't accept it in the entire area of the Central Bosnia and Herzegovina." Pelivan agreed, saying that Tudjman's proposed language seeking to legalise or legitimise Herceg-Bosna, quote, "would not pass on the government, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Pelivan continued: "Listen, we are talking about Herceg-Bosna here, a community as a political organisation. This government hasn't been established everywhere. The fact is that this may cause disapproval on the other side. Serbs will also request to have their government." My apologies to interpreters: "Serbs will also request to have their government." In fact, we know by now that that had already occurred. Having plainly and repeatedly said that Herceg-Bosna was not acceptable, Izetbegovic and the BiH delegation, due to Herceg-Bosna's aggressive actions over the past several months, were nonetheless faced with a fait accompli, which was certainly no accident. Herceg-Bosna had declared its existence. Herceg-Bosna had established a separate government. Herceg-Bosna had established its separate armed forces. Herceg-Bosna had seized power in municipality after municipality. It was a fait accompli. The most Izetbegovic could extract in the friendship agreement was the commitment by Tudjman that the Herceg-Bosna structures, the HVO civil structures, would, quote, "be made to conform as soon as possible with the constitutional juridical system of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." What else could he say? They already existed. So he signs an agreement and walks away, saying, Well, they are a fait accompli, but you commit to bringing them into compliance with our constitutional system, quote, "as soon as possible." The follow-up to the friendship meeting on both fronts, I think, is very telling, because contrary to what happens on the Herceg-Bosna side, you can actually see the BiH authorities trying to act in good faith. They're trying to carry out this friendship agreement. But as you'll see again, the Herceg-Bosnans will have none of it. Less than three weeks after the so-called friendship agreement was signed on 21 July, the BiH Presidency amended the BiH Law on Armed Forces in what the Prosecution submits was a prompt, reasonable, and bona fide effort to carry out the agreement. It affirmed that the HVO was part of the BiH state forces, to the extent that it truly was, if it was, subject and subordinate to the same single unified command, and, as such, that the HVO was a subordinated part of the BiH state armed forces. The decree adopted on 6th August 1992 amended Article 2 of the Law on the Armed Forces to state: "The Army of the Republic (hereinafter: the Army) constitutes the armed forces of the republic. "Units of the Croatian Defence Council constitute an integral part of the army, as well as other formations," and this is the critical language, "which put themselves under the single command of the army." The statutory language is fully consistent with not only the language of Section 6 of the friendship agreement but the entire concept of a unified armed force under a single unified command. After measuring -- again, measuring the words carefully, the friendship agreement says the HVO will have its representatives in the joint command of the armed forces. The carefully-measured words say nothing, again, about the HVO being a separate but equal army somehow related to the BiH state armed forces, but somehow marching to a different command with Boban as its supreme commander. You can't have two supreme commanders. You can't have the BiH Presidency, with Izetbegovic being the president of the Presidency, as supreme commander, and you can't have Mate Boban being supreme commander at the same time. Indeed, I would remind the Chamber there are already Bosnian Croats in senior positions in the BiH state armed forces, with the Croat Stjepan Siber being the number 2 commander of the ABiH, a Croat. The BiH Presidency's position, far from being disingenuous, as the Defence seems to suggest on occasion, was fully consistent with the HVO's own concept of a single armed force under one command, as reflected in one of the series of HVO orders that we saw in the spring of 1992; first from Boban, then from Roso, then there was another one from Blaskic, saying that only the HVO is legal. If you want to be part of us, you'll be completely subordinated to us. You'll wear our insignia, you'll take no orders, no commands from anyone else, et cetera. And we have that and we can see that in Roso's 8 May 1992 order in which he says, and this is from May of 1992: "1. The only legal military units in the territory of the HZ-HB are units of the HVO. "2. All other military units in the above territory must join the single defence system and recognise the HVO Main Staff as their supreme command. 3. Every member of the above military units must wear HVO insignia (badge on cap and canvass HVO sign on left sleeve)." Your Honours, how is it that the self-appointed political and military leaders of the self-declared Herceg-Bosna para-state could insist that any armed forces on its alleged territory must join, quote, "the single defence system" and must, quote, "recognise the HVO Main Staff as their supreme command," closed quote, and, quote, "must wear HVO insignia," while at the same time taking the position that the legal and legitimate Presidency of the internationally-recognised UN member state of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not require those who would be part of its legitimate state armed forces operating on its sovereign territory, which extended all the way, by the way, to the international border with Croatia, to, quote, "join the single defence system" and recognise the BiH Presidency as, quote, "their supreme command"? Sauce for the goose, sauce for the gander. In their sworn testimony, the accused Petkovic and the senior HVO commander and Defence witness Filipovic both made clear that the person they considered the supreme commander of the HVO was the president of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban. Confirming all aspects of an HVO organisational chart that he prepared for the Blaskic case, Petkovic repeatedly said concerning the box -- remember, the box on the chart said "supreme commander." Petkovic says, That's Mate Boban: "Yes, it's Mr. Mate Boban, this box which reads 'supreme commander.'" Petkovic testified that Boban was the HVO's supreme commander from the time that Petkovic arrived in Bosnia in April 1992 until February 1994, when Boban left that position. It was likewise put to Filipovic: "And then it says 'the Decree on armed forces stipulated that the commander-in-chief was at the head of the army. "Q. Do you agree? "A. Yes, if you mean the supreme commander who was Boban." An army, Your Honours, cannot serve two masters. Two armies cannot have two different supreme commanders and be the same army. Indeed, Filipovic himself plainly conceded, both in his Kordic testimony and in this case, that there three armies in BiH each serving, quote, "the interest of that side." Filipovic affirmed and adopted the following from his Kordic testimony: "We had three armies in Bosnia-Herzegovina: The Army of the Republika Srpska, which separated and took up arms to reach their objectives; then we had the Muslim side, which wore the green fezzes, had their own flags, had their own insignia; then we had the Croatian component or party and represented the interest of that side. "And if you're talking about the joint defence of Croats and Bosniaks, that is, Muslims, that was jointly but not the same. "At that time, we could not have had the same army. That was a purely theoretical concept." And I'd ask the Chamber, as you continue to consider this issue, to distinguish between sometimes allies and being the same army. There may, indeed, have been -- and, in fact, there were times when the HVO and the ABiH fought together against the Serbs. We've talked about that through the years. Being an ally does not make you part of the same army. The HVO and the ABiH, in the areas and during the times relevant to this case, were never the same army. Petkovic's own actions only three days after the BiH Presidency's 6 August decree speak volumes of the attitude on the HVO side. In contrast to but in the face of the BiH Presidency's adoption of the decree, amended decree, Herceg-Bosna simply continued its march toward a separate Croat space under separate Croat control and excluded or attempted to exclude all other armed forces from its territory. On 10 August 1992, Petkovic ordered Herceg-Bosna military police and civilian police commanders to, quote: "Use all available HVO, civilian, and military police forces to prevent any military units other than the HVO from entering your area of responsibility." Any. "This is solely HVO territory. None others are welcome, none others will be accepted. You are to advise this staff on the presence of any unit other than the HVO." P00377. Simply put, the HVO had no intention of subordinating itself to the command of the BiH Presidency in the summer or fall of 1992 or any time during 1993, not seriously, not in good faith, not genuinely. Now, there was also follow-up to the friendship meeting on the political side. We've talked about the military. Remember the language which talked about to bring the Herceg-Bosna structures as soon as possible into compliance with Bosnia's constitutional juridical system? Well, Mr. Izetbegovic and the BiH Presidency develops the notion of, during this wartime situation, of a new organisation based on districts. This started in August 1992, which ordered the organisation of BiH into initially seven and later ten districts. The Herceg-Bosnans, of course, were opposed to this, as they were opposed to BiH authorities doing anything in Herceg-Bosna. Stojic reported at a meeting of the HZ-HB Presidency on the 14th of August -- this is just a couple of weeks -- several weeks, not later. Stojic has attended a meeting with some BiH ministers, and he goes back and reports to the BiH -- excuse me, to the HZ-HB Presidency on the 14th of August. He had met with BiH ministers the day before at which the BiH ministers had offered co-operation in fighting together against the Serbs, but had rejected ethnic units or cantons. Stojic reported in the minutes of that meeting: "After this meeting, the conclusion is there can be no agreement with the Muslims." That's Stojic on the 14th of August, 1992. In fact, organisation of all of the proposed BiH districts went forward during the fall of 1992 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott. Is there a quota for this last quotation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, excuse me. It's P00391.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're welcome. In fact, organisation of all the proposed BiH districts went forward during the fall of 1992 and thereafter, except for the Mostar and Livno districts, which were located, of course, on Herceg-Bosna's so-called territory. Indeed, jumping ahead to 1993 just for a moment, when the BiH authorities made further attempts to establish the Mostar and Livno districts in the first quarter of 1993, Prlic and the Herceg-Bosna leader vociferously opposed them as contrary -- plainly contrary to the Greater Croatian banovina project. Just as the Herceg-Bosnans have no bona fide intentions of making the HVO military part of the BiH state armed forces under the BiH's Presidency's control, they likewise had no intention of dismantling Herceg-Bosna or bringing it into conformity with the legal and juridical system of Bosnia-Herzegovina, quote, "as soon as possible." That was not part of the agenda. In fact, the evidence will show that Boban, Prlic, and Herceg-Bosnans continued to march as fast as possible in the opposite direction, not ameliorating, not softening their positions in the face of all the opposition from the international community and from the Muslims and from the BiH authorities, not saying -- not rethinking their position, but going hard and fast in the opposite direction. By July 1992, the Herceg-Bosnan leadership knew that it continued to face troublesome opposition and annoying competition, not only from the BiH Presidency against Muslims, but from many moderate Croats, including the moderate parts of the HDZ-BiH party and from two Croat organisations called the Croatian Party of Rights and its Croatian Defence forces or HOS. Boban, Praljak, and the others knew that it would be difficult to move forward and consolidate their power further unless and until these other factions -- competing factions and forces were silenced or side-lined. Now, talking about the party, we've talked a bit this afternoon about -- well, we knew about Kljuic, who's gone, effectively. We know about Milenko Brkic, another moderate who has now been side-lined, has a big fight with Tudjman at the July meeting, and that's continuing. While people like Boban, Boras, and Kordic often talked about the HDZ-BiH as their party, their party, by mid-1992 the HDZ Bosnian branch had not, in fact, proven to be an entirely reliable vehicle for the Herceg-Bosnans to accomplish their work, at least not until the hard-liners fully consolidated their control in November -- some months from now in November of 1992. Party leaders and members like Kljuic, Brkic, and others had proven difficult for Boban and his Herceg-Bosna compatriots, so that the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership had largely abandoned the party by the late spring of 1992. Or, to put it differently, it was content to let it sit there, essentially, inactive. At the Zagreb meeting on 5 July 1992, if you remember, the acting HDZ president, Brkic, had put to Tudjman that some people were already asking if the work of the party had been suspended: "People are asking, should we have a convention?" In fact, Tudjman, himself, discouraged calling an HDZ-BiH convention during this time, and the Prosecution submits that it was exactly for these reasons. Calling a meeting -- calling an HDZ convention in Bosnia, with people -- with the likes of Kljuic and Brkic and other moderates still in top party positions would be dangerous. The HDZ-BiH official Zdenko Cosic confirmed at a meeting with Tudjman at meeting with Tudjman on 17th September 1992 that Tudjman had expressed reservations about calling a convention, as Brkic had suggested, saying, quote, "it was not really desirable to call a convention at such times." That's from P00498. The accused Petkovic and Defence witness Filipovic confirmed that by mid-1992, the HDZ-BiH was no longer active or any real factor during the war. Petkovic testified: "... the HDZ had frozen its activities. I don't think that it had dismantled itself, but it had frozen its activities. "So the HDZ didn't gather at any levels at the lower, mid levels, or higher levels. So in the course of the war, it quite simply ceased to operate. " ... it did not gather, it did not work, it didn't assemble, and it didn't take any decisions. Now, I'm going to pause here, because maybe, ultimately, we may some times by noting some of these issues as we go rather than circling -- perhaps circling back to them tomorrow. One of the other claims that we've heard from the various Defence teams from time to time is, Where are these other alternative bases of power? You know, Prlic wasn't responsible, the real power was in the party, or the real power was over here, or the real power was in the municipalities. And we're going to try to touch on all those and explain to Your Honours why none of those were true. Well, this is one of them, because when they point the finger, and when maybe they get up in the next two weeks and say, Well, you know, it was really the HDZ-BiH party that had the power, uh-uh, no, the party wasn't even operating during this period. Petkovic and Filipovic, one accused, one Defence witness, both confirmed party inactive, not doing anything, not a power base during this time-period. The HVO commander Filipovic says: "In the Kordic case --" I put to him: "Q. In the Kordic case, you testified and you said that the political party known as the HDZ-BiH, the Bosnian wing of the HDZ, that that political party as of June 1992 was not active, that it had at least effectively ceased to exist. Would you stand by that testimony today? "A. In that area in which I was in, it was stated that it froze its activity. "Q. All right. And --" Apologies: "And in another place, in your same testimony on that, you said: 'In the summer of 1992, the parties officially ceased to function.' So that relates to what you just told us just now also? "A. Yes, that it froze their actions. They were on ice." Petkovic comes back to it and even actually takes it even further. This is his testimony in this case. Actually, we've jumped a slide, I think. Sorry, Your Honour, I have some technical -- all right. My apologies. My mistake, as always. Thank you, Skye. Petkovic testifies: "Your testimony in Kordic, at page 268 '04-05 ... "Q. Some of the international observers have speculated that the HVO Army affairs were subject to pervasive political control exerted by the HDZ-BiH. Is that true, that there was such control exerted by the political party?" Milivoj Petkovic, under oath: "Your Honours, that is not true. It is another matter that our supreme commander ..." Note that, again confirming who the supreme commander was, not Izetbegovic. "... our supreme commander, Mate Boban ... was the number one man -- number one in the HDZ." He was the number one in the party, which depending on the time wasn't necessarily true, at least not de jure: "But I do not see that the HDZ ever ran the army or the HDZ, as such, as a party, imposed itself on the military. And as far as I know, I think the work of the party was frozen for a while. "Q. Which is actually consistent with what you said just a moment ago; correct? "A. Yes, that's correct." The HDZ was not functioning, was inactive, was on ice, was frozen, is not an alternative power base. It is not anyone or anything that the accused can point to as being responsible for what happened in Herceg-Bosna. Now, they also needed to eliminate this organisation called HOS because it was also being troublesome. Bosnian Croat opposition to or competition with Herceg-Bosna was not limited to the HDZ-BiH or its more moderate factions. There was also something called the Croatian Party of Rights and its military wing known as the Croatian Defence Forces or HOS, which were the HDZ's and HVO's principal rivals for Croat members and their support in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Important point: Ideologically, HOS differed from the Herceg-Bosnans in a very important way, in that HOS favoured a single shared Croat-Muslim BiH, rather than the Serb-Croat partition which Tudjman and the Herceg-Bosnians supported. HOS was more closely aligned with the BiH authorities and the BH state armed forces. HOS and its leader, Blaz Kraljevic, acknowledged the BiH authorities in Sarajevo, rather than the Herceg-Bosnans in Grude and Mostar, and recognised Izetbegovic, not Boban, as supreme commander. The Defence Witness Jurcevic observed in his report that Kraljevic, quote -- so this is coming from a Defence witness: "Kraljevic supported co-operation between the Croats and the Muslims and Bosniaks. In early August 1992, the government in Sarajevo appointed General Kraljevic a member of the BH Army Main Staff." Was the ABiH -- was Izetbegovic willing to put senior Croats in senior positions of command if they were willing to do so and willing to be subordinate to his authority? Yes, he was, and we have HOS and Blaz Kraljevic as proof of that. For these reasons, HOS was popular with Muslims as well as Croats, and in many municipalities, such as Zenica, there were more Muslims than Croats in HOS. HOS was a formidable-enough competitor that the HVO, in the summer of 1992, feared that HOS might even become the dominant force in such places as Capljina and Ljubuski. It is easy to see from these circumstances that HOS, as a military-capable Croat organisation that was much more closely oriented toward the BiH authorities in Sarajevo, rather than Herceg-Bosna, was seen by Boban, Praljak, and others as a threat. Because of this, on 9 August 1992, Blaz Kraljevic and eight other HOS members were killed in ambush at Krusevo, near Mostar. The Defence witness Jurcevic, again Mr. Jurcevic, testified that this part of his report was completely accurate, and this is what he said: "Due to the many differences between parts of the HVO and the HOS, Kraljevic was soon killed in an ambush near Mostar. "At that point, an all-out armed conflict between the HOS and the HVO was avoided by an agreement signed on 23 August 1992 by Mate Boban and the chief of the Main Staff of the HOS (Ante Prkacin). "After this, the HOS was completely disbanded when groups or individual members transferred to the HVO or the BH Army." After Kraljevic's assassination, the HVO quickly took over many HOS units. It is noteworthy that the man who was Blaz Kraljevic's deputy, Ivica Primorac, had, just prior to his defection from HOS to the HVO, and just shortly before Kraljevic's murder, met several times a Mate Sarlija, also known as Daidza, and with Slobodan Praljak, and had also spoken with Boban. The same Primorac went on to become the assistant chief of the HVO Main Staff for professional units and continued in this post until August of 1993. He goes from deputy commander of HOS, the Prosecution submits, makes a deal with the HVO, and is rewarded with a senior position in the HVO military. As confirmed by the Defence witness Jurcevic, soon after Primorac defected from HOS to the HVO and Kraljevic was murdered, much of HOS was subordinated to the HVO in the agreement signed by Boban. Slobodan Praljak confirmed to Franjo Tudjman that he, that is, Praljak, was, quote, "personally involved with Prkacin" in the, quote, "destruction of HOS." In a meeting in Tudjman's office on the 26th of September, 1992, when the Croatian president was upset with Prkacin for calling himself a, quote, "general" in the Croatian Army, and seemed to be looking to punish him, Praljak came to Prkacin's defence: "Mr. President, please, I'd like to say that it is not so simple. Openly speaking --" "Openly speaking, we have used Mr. Prkacin, I personally and in co-operation with others, for destruction of the HOS down there. He has done a good job down there." It was, indeed, a good job for Praljak and the Herceg-Bosnans. HOS had been destroyed; mission accomplished. By mid-1992, Your Honours, the patterns, practices, and characteristics of ethnic cleansing in the former Yugoslavia were already well known and widely reported. In his report dated the 27th of October, 1992, the UN special rapporteur, Mazowiecki, stated: "The special rapporteur shares the view of other observers that the principal objective of the military conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina is the establishment of ethnically-homogeneous regions. Ethnic cleansing does not appear to be a consequence of the war, but rather its goal. This goal, to a large extent, has already been achieved through killings, beatings, rape, destruction of houses, and threats." In his report titled "The Characteristics and Patterns of the Balkan Conflicts as Widely Known and Reported by the Latter Part of 1992," the Prosecution expert witness Nicholas Miller addressed the following questions -- that report, by the way, is Exhibit P10239. Miller answered the following questions that had been posed to him: "Q. What characteristics and patterns or practices in the wars in the former Yugoslavia were extensively reported, widely known, and publicly recognised by the middle and latter parts of 1992?" Next question: "Q. Given the precedent of the war in Croatia in the first months of war in Bosnia, would ethnic violence against civilians in the form of murder, expulsions, and rape, likely ensue?" Miller answered that: "The civilian toll of acts of persecution, attacks, and forcible population transfers was, in fact, widely known in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992." That: "The attempt to subjugate populations and/or take territory was substantially likely to result in violence against civilians, including killings, widespread destruction, forced expulsions, and other criminal acts." And that: "Such acts were already manifested during the conflict in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina by and beyond the latter part of 1992." Miller reported that in the Balkan wars of the 1990s, quote, "civilians became a particular focus of attention of warring parties, who were not merely trying to defeat an enemy, but were trying to clear territory of one or the other ethnic group either entirely or in large measure." In this way, quote, "ethnicity was the fuel of the conflict," and, quote, "territorial conquest and cleansing was the goal." The large-scale armed violence was not accidentally ethnic but instead, quote, "the issue in these conflicts was, in fact, ethnicity." Certain types of behaviour or practices became well known and predictable: "One regular theme and one which was well publicised internationally and locally was the barricaded town or village as the site of ethnic struggle." If I might submit, the use of the word "barricaded town," I think, might be described as a siege. Throughout 1991 and by the summer and autumn of 1992, quote, "the dominant characteristics of a conflict based on ethnicity and the practices and patterns of behaviour involved in such conflict became and were widely reported, publicly recognised, and well understood. Attacks on civilians, forcible population transfers, and large-scale detentions were already a known part of what was already being called and had already been coined 'ethnic cleansing.'" By mid-1992, there was an increasing body of United Nations resolutions, reports, and other UN communications describing with great concern the developments and characteristics of the Yugoslav conflicts. Another common story in the press coverage at the time was the, quote, "barbarous treatment of captives." Yet another was that refugees and displaced persons had become pawns and that, quote, "refugee resettlement had become a tool in ethnic cleansing." As Mazowiecki reported on 28 August 1992: "The detention of civilians is clearly being used as a method of pressuring them to leave the territory. In many cases, after agreeing to leave, they are obliged to sign documents renouncing their claim to their homes and other property, or indicating that they agree to donate their property to the local government." All of these phenomena were widely reported, well understood, and publicly recognised by the end of 1991. In this way, quote, "the political and military leaders and various factions of the Serbian, Croatian, and Muslim groups or organisations must have known or had every reason to believe that what a continuation and expansion of the conflicts would bring. The goal of territorial partition of Bosnia based largely on ethnicity was stated, foreseen, and, indeed, virtually taken for granted by Croatian and Serbian political and military leaders by early 1992. In this context, in this information environment, in Western Herzegovina, Croatian political and military leaders from Croatia and Bosnia began to prepare for a war that they saw as both inevitable and desirable." And that was a quote from P10239, page 11. As Miller stated in his report: "To put it succinctly, the war in Bosnia proceeded predictably according to a script of patterns and practices already written in Croatia, but with more intensity." In fact, by mid-1992 -- now, remember, we're still in 1992. We haven't even gotten to 1993 yet. In fact, by mid-1992, ethnic cleansing in Herzegovina, itself, was already widely reported. A writer for "Vreme" reported in August 1992 that in July 1992, Red Cross representatives visited camps and prisons in Mostar, Ljubuski, and Capljina, and that in the years since the conflict began, quote, "violations of humanitarian law and human rights have been committed by all sides in the conflict and had become a practice, particularly as far as the civilian population is concerned." By August 1992, the existence of HVO -- August 1992, the existence of HVO camps at Ljubuski and Capljina was known in the West. The fact that the UN special rapporteur, Mazowiecki, by mid-1992 was already reporting on the existence and operation of four detention camps on "Bosnian Croat territory (Livno, Mostar, Orasje, and Rascani) is telling." Miller reported: "The Croatian media reported widely on the entire spectrum of events. The Serbian and international press did as well. Any moderately-informed person living and working in the former Yugoslavia could not but have known of these developments and reports and the characteristics and practices involved in the Balkan conflict." As an example, Franjo Tudjman, himself, in a meeting with Herceg-Bosna leaders, including Mr. Prlic, on the 17th of September, 1992, expressly noted, quote, "this barbarity that is unfolding in Bosnia and Herzegovina" involving, quote, "mutual extermination." Indeed, the actions of the warring sides through the middle of 1992 clearly indicated that killings of civilians, forced expulsion, and widespread destruction would ensue should any ethnic group try to subrogate another in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As discussed earlier, the American diplomat Warren Zimmerman had by this time already warned Franjo Tudjman where his Bosnian policy would lead and what would result from them: "There will be war in Bosnia if you try to divide it. Don't you think the Muslims will react? What you propose ignores the rights of a large share of Bosnia's population." By the end of July 1992, several things were clear. Except for the occasional shell or local incident, all significant fighting, with a few exceptions, between the Serbs and the Croats in the wider Mostar region was over, with the Trial Chamber establishing the adjudicated fact that, quote, "most Serbs had left or been driven out of Mostar." Jadranko Prlic confirmed this some weeks later in a meeting with Tudjman on the 17th of September, 1992, where he reported: "We did not enter a single Serb village, nor do we want a single Serbian village." The real conflict, both in Herzegovina and in many parts of Central Bosnia, was now between the Croats and Muslims, as the Trial Chamber has determined by a number of adjudicated facts. It was increasingly clear that the BH authorities and the Muslims, generally, with some exceptions, did not accept Herceg-Bosna and, in fact, were increasingly opposed to it. In a call for co-operation in mid-July 1992, the Muslim leadership in and around Mostar, including the mufti, Sead Smajkic, Ismet Hadziosmanovic, Mira Rajic and Miro Mahmutcehajic, protested the increasingly mono-ethnic nature of the HVO administration. They warned that there had been no agreement, quote, "on the status of the predominantly Muslim municipalities (Konjic, Jablanica, Mostar and Stolac)." They urged that Muslim and Croat fighters be given equal status, that a multi-ethnic joint command be established, and that both a civilian and military police also be organised on a proportional basis, quote, "in line with the Statute of the Armed Forces of the RBiH," the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Muslim leaders asked for the recognition of both Bosnian and Croatia as official languages, and that the symbols of the Republic of Bosnia and Hercegovina be introduced. Imagine that, the symbols of that sovereign country actually being re-introduced on its sovereign territory. They called for both ethnic groups to be involved in setting the university curriculum and for university teachers to be selected on the basis of equality. They also called for captured JNA property to be allocated in line with the regulations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Unfortunately, these requests fell on deaf HVO ears and were simply ignored, further adding to the mounting tensions that would lead to open conflict. Similar protests and requests were made in a petition from the Muslims of Herzegovina on 8 August 1992. They advocated, quote, "the integral and indivisible state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and did not recognise any parastatal creations." The petition called for the use of the BiH flag and coat of arms as well as the introduction of total equality of the Bosnian language with the Croatia and Serbian languages. Many of the same things were said again, but with greater urgency, in the SDA Regional Committee president's 14 September 1992 letter to the president of the HZ-HB, Mr. Boban; to the president of the HZ-HB government, that is, Jadranko Prlic; to the president of the party, HDZ BiH; and the president in Mostar HVO government, Jadran Topic. In addition to restating demands for common symbols and insignia, equality in the military, and the use of the BiH flag, they also asked for freedom of movement for all citizens and equal treatment at customs crossings. It was abundantly clear and plainly known to Tudjman and the Herceg-Bosna political and military leadership that Izetbegovic, the BiH authorities, and Muslims, generally, and, indeed, many moderate Croats, did not accept Herceg-Bosna and had not given the assents or agreements that Tudjman and the others might have hoped for.
