In statement after statement from July 1992 forward, these leaders, including Prlic, Petkovic, Praljak and others, recognised that Herceg-Bosna's relationships with the Muslims were poor, that they had no agreement with the Muslims, that open conflict was foreseeable and even inevitable, with Tudjman's policies and the Herceg-Bosna para-state on a collision course with the Muslim opposition. The accused Petkovic had already given an important briefing to the HZ-HB Presidency on 3 July 1992, before the important 5 July and 21 July Tudjman meetings, stating that in most of Herceg-Bosna's territory -- this was Petkovic - relations with the Muslims, who he described -- his words were "the minority ethnic group in these parts," a patently false statement. They were not the minority group in Stolac, they were not the minority group in Jablanica, they were not the minority group in Konjic. But, nonetheless, Petkovic said the relationships with the Muslims were poor. The HDZ BiH acting president, Brkic, had told Tudjman on 5 July that there had been much recklessness: "Relations with Muslims are growing more complicated." Izetbegovic again had plainly rejected Herceg-Bosna at the 21 July friendship meeting. Brkic agreed, Pelivan agreed. The words to Tudjman and the Herceg-Bosnians leadership, including these men, was, We're not buying it, we don't accept Herceg-Bosna. Don't go there, because if you go there, there's going to be a war. And as I've just spent 10 minutes telling you about, the patterns and practices of ethnic cleansing are going to come about because that was -- those were the patterns and practices and characteristics of this conflict. If you're buying into war here, gentlemen, the Muslims don't agree, they done accept Herceg-Bosna, and if you push your agenda, that's where this is headed. As I mentioned earlier, Stojic had already told the HZ-HB Presidency, after a meeting with the BiH authorities on the 14th of August, there can be no agreement with the Muslims. In another meeting in Zagreb on 29 August 1992, involving both Tudjman and Izetbegovic, two fundamental facts were once again clear. First, it was Tudjman who was calling the shots on the Croat side, with Boban occasionally joining the dialogue but always deferring to Tudjman. And, second, there was still no political agreement between the Croats and Muslims as to Herceg-Bosna. Tudjman and Boban, however, still insisted on a separate Croat space, with Croat sovereignty there: "We want to have the space down there with relative authority, the authority of the Croat people." That comes from P00414. Tudjman tried once again to purchase Izetbegovic's acceptance of Herceg-Bosna by linking it to the HVO's participation in a joint command with Sarajevo. Now, this is telling again. Remember all this talk, We want to be part of the single joint army, and we all want to be a part of the same big family of armies. The fact that that was not the case is what Tudjman does here, If you accept Herceg-Bosna, the HVO will join you. That's the condition precedent. If you accept Herceg-Bosna, then we'll join up with you. Tudjman says: "An agreement on joint command should be definitely reached. However, such a command is not possible if there is no previous agreement between the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia. It means this is related to a general political solution." That, again, is from P00414. In a sense, and whether he intended it or not, Tudjman had made the agenda finally perfectly clear. The HVO will participate in a joint command with the BiH state armed forces, but only if you first give us Herceg-Bosna. There was, once again, a fundamental clash between a unified, multi-ethnic Bosnia of equal citizens and the model of a separate ethnic space with separate sovereignty and control. On 11 September 1992, while meeting with Tudjman to discuss the military situation in Bosnia, one of Mr. Praljak's trips to report back to Tudjman in Zagreb, Praljak tells Tudjman and Susak, quote: "War with the Muslims can be anticipated." Now, that's 11 September 1992. It's about six weeks before Prozor at the end of October. So Praljak goes back to Zagreb knowing there's no agreement with the Muslims, that conflict is inevitable, and says -- and reports back to his boss, Tudjman: "War with the Muslims can be anticipated." Six weeks before Prozor. Far from being satisfied, Susak simply responded as if to say to Praljak, Tell us something we don't already know. Susak says back -- responds to Praljak: "We have been aware of that for over a week now, and we have made preparations on what needs to be done. Mr. Praljak, we're already a week ahead of you. We know a war with the Muslims is coming, and we've already started the preparations a week ago." That comes from P00466, page 51. Only a few days later on 17 September 1992, Tudjman held another important meeting with a number of senior advisers and various Herceg-Bosna HVO leaders, including Boban and Prlic. Tudjman plainly understood that he had achieved no agreement with Izetbegovic and that his policy of sending Croatian troops into Bosnia was seriously exposed. This is Tudjman from P00498, pages 69 to 72: "Here at this table --" Sitting in the presidential offices in Zagreb, Here at this table, gentlemen: "Here at this table we had long discussions where Izetbegovic insisted that the HVO be recognised as a military, not political power of the people ... when we signed the agreement here -- Izetbegovic did not want a military agreement ... As it is, not only are we left without it ... but, let me ask you, show me a citizen of Croatia who wants to go to war, to an illegal war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. How can we take to court our soldier who refuses to go --" By the way, these are supposed to be the volunteers: "How can we take to court our soldier who refuses to go when we are saying that only volunteers go? Therefore, we find ourselves in a delicate situation, both with respect to our own folk, our own people, and particularly with respect to the world. So he did not want to sign the agreement," Izetbegovic. "Why? Ask him." That's Tudjman's attitude at this time in mid-September. I don't have the agreement, we don't have cover, we are conducting an illegal war in Bosnia. Why doesn't he sign the agreement? I don't know. Ask him. Tudjman, himself, in explicitly discussing the so-called friendship agreement at a 26 September 1992 meeting of Croatia's National Defence Council -- we're not talking about the local Boy Scouts; we're talking about Croatia's National Defence Council -- acknowledged still again the absence of a political agreement when he bemoaned the Muslims' unwillingness to accept the idea of parallel structures, referring to the earlier negotiations: "In the end, when we signed that agreement --" The July so-called friendship agreement: "In the end, when we signed that agreement, we proposed a military clause that Izetbegovic rejected ... "I said that since we already talked about that, that we didn't want to limit ourselves just to the military co-operation, that as far as Croatia is concerned, we should not concentrate on a lengthy war, but also on a political solution. "Then we made a draft which he did sign, but it was just that he could get a possibility to supply over our territory." Apparently thinking it was safe to say so among friends, Tudjman expressed a "how dare they" attitude or a "how dare they" annoyance that the BiH government would actually be so bold as to want to exercise sovereignty on its own territory, quote, "even in those areas, Croatian areas, where the HVO has control." P00524, page 6. Croatian Defence Minister Susak pipes in immediately to the boss concerning events in a foreign country, not his own, quickly assured Tudjman, We won't allow that. They want to exercise sovereignty on that territory of Herceg-Bosna. Mr. President, we won't allow that. Tudjman concluded the issue with words that were as clear as noon on a spring day: "We will openly tell Izetbegovic, when he comes here, what we said in the beginning. There can be no discussion about them establishing military and civilian government in areas that used to be within the Croatian Banovina." Praljak proudly admitted to the Bosnian Serb leader Ratko Mladic, in a meeting on 5 October 1992, also involving Prlic and Stojic -- so you had -- at the same meeting with Ratko Mladic on the 5th of October, you have Praljak, Prlic and Stojic. And Praljak says, There's no agreement, the Croats have no agreement with Izetbegovic. The agreement between -- he abbreviates "T" for "Tudjman" and "AI," "AI" being Alija Izetbegovic, we submit -- does not contain anything, it's an empty agreement. Looking back, Tudjman confirmed more than a year later, in a meeting on 21 September 1993, that he had not reached any agreement with Izetbegovic in July 1992: "We tried to sign -- as you know, I signed an agreement with the Muslims in the summer of last year. We proposed a military agreement to Izetbegovic that would allow the legal engagement of the army. He did not accept it. Since we did not have a military agreement, we were in a delicate position with our Croatian soldiers. We are at war, and we must not say we are at war. However, we are sending them there. The people would not have it, and they deserted, et cetera. We cannot take them to court, because that is the way it is, politically." In short, by at least July/August 1992, Tudjman, Susak and the Herceg-Bosna HVO political and military leaders, including the accused, knew or had every reason to know the nature and circumstances of the conflicts surrounding them and the fact that ethnic violence had taken a strong and tragic hold on the former Yugoslavia by this time, with known patterns of attacks on towns and villages, mass expulsions, wide-scale destruction, the confinement and mistreatments of prisoners, and the movement of populations, including refugees and other displaced persons. As Miller reported: "Any moderately-informed person living and working in the former Yugoslavia could not but have known of these developments and reports and the characteristics and practices involved in the Balkan conflict." The actions of the warring sides through the middle of 1992 showed very plainly that killings of civilians, forced expulsions, and widespread destruction would ensue should any ethnic group try to subjugate another in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Further, Tudjman, Susak and the Herceg-Bosna HVO political and military leaders, including the accused, knew that Izetbegovic, the BiH state authorities and the vast majority of Muslims did not accept Herceg-Bosna, and were, in fact, becoming ever more vocal, ever more active, in their opposition to it. Tudjman and the others knew they had no political agreement with the Muslims. Tudjman and the accused faced a decision point. And I'll tell the Chamber, I propose to end here on this point this evening, but I'm being very transparent. This is what we consider a fundamental point in the chronology. This is a turning point. By August/September 1992, before Prozor in October, Tudjman and the others knew they had no political agreement with the Muslims. Tudjman and these accused faced a decision point. Herceg-Bosna and the Banovina were not going to be accomplished peacefully. Muslims were not going to go peacefully. The BiH authorities and Muslims were not going to lay down. They would not simply go along. Tudjman and the accused could either back away from their project, perhaps even thinking or saying to themselves, Well, nice try, boys, but it didn't work, or they could take it to the next level, knowing that if they did so, the same and even worse phenomena of ethnic death, destruction and displacement that were already occurring all around them would follow from and be the horrible consequences of their decision. Tudjman and the accused could either back away from the project, Nice try, or they could take it to the next level. Unfortunately for tens of thousands of Muslims and Croats who would be affected one way or another, losing sons and daughters, fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters, and everything they had, Tudjman and the accused chose the latter course, leading to increased tensions and escalating conflicts, which resulted only a few weeks later in the crimes at Prozor in late October 1992 and would, tragically, take the parties into war in 1993. Thank you, Your Honours.
